findings.title: Verify and pin install.sh before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL ... | sh` downloads and executes arbitrary code from a hardcoded URL at image build time with no checksum, signature, or version pinning, and `-L` follows redirects. Whoever controls the host (or any redirect target / MITM) gets arbitrary code execution inside the build with full environment access, and the script's integrity is never checked or recorded anywhere in the repo (rg for install.sh/sha256/verify found nothing).

findings.title: Fail build when install.sh download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A failed download is silently turned into a successful build: `-s` suppresses curl's error output, and without `set -e`/`pipefail` (alpine:3.18's `/bin/sh` is busybox ash, which has no pipefail) the pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s — empty input exits 0. A 404, timeout, or DNS failure therefore yields an image that built fine but is missing whatever install.sh was supposed to install, indistinguishable from a real success.

findings.title: Pin and verify remote install.sh; never curl|sh as root
findings.whyItBreaks: The build fetches an unpinned, unverified remote script and executes it as root inside the image. The URL is example.com, IANA's placeholder domain (it serves its fixed 'Example Domain' page for any path and is not a distribution endpoint), so the artifact being executed is not the installer the line claims to run. There is no checksum, signature, or version pin, and -L follows redirects without a scheme restriction, so the executed payload is whatever the remote returns at build time — an unbounded supply-chain trust decision baked into the image with no provenance.

findings.title: curl -sL failure is silent: pipeline exits 0, install never happens
findings.whyItBreaks: -s silences curl's error output and the pipeline's exit status is sh's (Docker runs RUN via /bin/sh -c; no set -o pipefail and no set -e in this shell). On a failed fetch (DNS/network/TLS error), curl emits nothing to the pipe, sh reads empty stdin and exits 0, so the RUN succeeds and the layer is committed even though nothing was installed — the image silently ships without the component this step was meant to add, and the builder (docker build) sees success, making the failure indistinguishable from a real install.

findings.title: Build executes unverified remote script (curl | sh)
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN step downloads https://example.com/install.sh and executes it directly with sh in the image build (as root, with the build environment's network/secrets, and no integrity check). No pinned version or commit SHA, no checksum, no signature, no pinned TLS/trust. Anyone who can influence that URL (DNS, CDN, MITM of the unverified origin, or future owner of the domain) gets code execution inside the build, which typically also has registry push credentials. Additionally the URL is a placeholder domain (example.com does not host install.sh), so the step is non-functional and non-reproducible: every rebuild re-fetches an unpinned artifact.

findings.title: curl failure is silently discarded by pipe-to-sh
findings.whyItBreaks: curl's exit status is never checked: the pipeline's exit status is sh's, and curl runs with -s (no error output) and without -f (HTTP errors like 404 are not treated as failure). On a network/DNS/TLS/connection failure, curl writes nothing to stdout and exits non-zero, sh reads an empty stdin and exits 0, so the RUN layer succeeds and the build silently produces an image without the tool this step promises to install. On an HTTP 404 the 404 page is piped into sh, causing a confusing sh syntax error. In the base image there was no such install promise, so this change both adds the promise and makes its failure indistinguishable from success; the failure signal never reaches the build.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault calls Load(key, m) and discards the error with the blank identifier, always returning v. For a missing key Load returns ("", ErrMissing); for a present key with an empty-string value Load returns ("", nil). Both paths yield "" from LoadOrDefault, so a caller cannot distinguish 'key absent' from 'key present with value ""' — failure is mapped to a legitimate stored value and the error signal is permanently lost. This is an exported public API of a generic string-map store (empty strings are fully representable), so every future caller is forced to treat missing-key as an empty value, reproducing the classic get-default trap where a defaulted empty string is persisted, reported, or acted on as real data.

findings.title: Exported LoadOrDefault discards error, conflates absent key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is a new exported API that does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns v. Load's only failure mode is ErrMissing, which is also the only situation where the value is indistinguishable from a legitimate stored value: a key explicitly mapped to "" returns ("", nil), while an absent key returns ("", ErrMissing) — LoadOrDefault maps both to "". Every future caller of this public function is forced to conflate "key absent" with "stored empty string" and cannot supply their own default, so silently-dropped configuration/data can read as a legitimate empty value. Additionally, any future error added to Load (e.g. backend/IO failure) would be silently converted to "" with no trace, making persisted wrong-data indistinguishable from a real value. The name implies "or default" but the default is an undocumented hardcoded zero value with no doc comment stating the semantics.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing; missing and empty values conflated
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR adds an exported wrapper that discards Load's error signal with `v, _ :=`. Load's whole point is to distinguish 'key not in map' (returns "", ErrMissing @store.go:10) from 'key present with empty-string value' (returns "", nil @store.go:12). LoadOrDefault returns "" in both cases, so any caller is forced to conflate load failure with a legitimate stored empty value. The store's error channel is a public contract (ErrMissing is exported), and this wrapper silently removes it from every future caller. There are no in-repo callers yet, but for an exported/public swallow site the defective API contract is the defect itself — it ships now, forcing every eventual caller to treat failure as a real value.

findings.title: Run returns before results delivered; breaks exported sync contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version blocked in the loop and did not return until every `results <- j * 2` send completed, so a caller could safely do `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` (or read the buffer) and see all results, in input order. Head version launches one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no WaitGroup, no close, and no done channel; ctx is not used for cancellation. Trivially natural caller patterns now break: (1) `Run(...); close(results)` races the in-flight goroutines and panics 'send on closed channel'; (2) a caller that stops reading after Run returns leaves every still-pending goroutine blocked forever on `results <-`, leaking one goroutine per unread job and losing those results; (3) with a buffered channel sized to len(jobs), Run returns before the buffer is filled, so a post-return read sees an empty/partial buffer; (4) delivery order is nondeterministic and no longer matches job order, breaking index-zipping consumers. The loop-variable capture is handled correctly (j passed by value), so the defect is the removed completion/ordering guarantee, not capture.

findings.title: Run returns before results delivered; leaks and races on channel
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior: Run(ctx, jobs, results) returns only after all len(jobs) sends completed, in jobs order. Head behavior: one goroutine is spawned per job and Run returns immediately; there is no WaitGroup, done channel, or close, and ctx is ignored, so nothing joins the goroutines. Concrete breakages for any caller of this exported API: (1) a caller that treats Run's return as completion and then closes results does close(results) while sends are still in flight -> 'send on closed channel' panic (goroutines run past Run's return; Run never synchronizes with them). (2) A caller that proceeds after Run and reads a buffered channel sees 0..N-1 values instead of N -> work silently lost; with an unbuffered channel and a receiver that starts later or stops early, the spawned goroutines block forever on results <- and leak silently, since Run returned nil and there is no way to observe the failure (the chan<- int signature also prevents the callee from closing to signal completion). (3) Result delivery order is now scheduler-dependent instead of deterministic in-order, breaking any consumer that matches results to job indices. The minimal remediation is to keep sends synchronous; if concurrency is intended, Run must join the goroutines (sync.WaitGroup) before returning and the ordering guarantee must be addressed, otherwise the function's de facto contract 'returns after all results are delivered' is broken.

findings.title: Run returns before results delivered; add wait/close synchronization
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code blocked on `results <- j*2`, so when Run returned, all len(jobs) results had been received; callers could immediately close(results) or treat return as done. The diff wraps each send in a goroutine and returns immediately: (1) a caller that closes `results` after Run returns (safe before) now races in-flight sends -> runtime panic "send on closed channel" from an unrecovered goroutine, crashing the program; (2) a caller that stops reading after Run returns (read timeout, ctx.Done, early exit) leaves every not-yet-scheduled goroutine blocked forever on the unbuffered send -> N goroutines leaked and job results silently lost; (3) no happens-before edge exists between Run returning and the sends, and the API offers no replacement completion signal (no close, no done channel, ctx is not consulted), so callers can no longer distinguish "all results delivered" from "nothing sent yet".

findings.title: Log() accepts tag but never emits it
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `tag ...string` to the exported package function `logger.Log`, which is a contract carrier promising optional tagging of the log line. The body still executes only `println(message)` — the tag is unconditionally discarded. Any caller (this is a public package function; the whole repo is just this source file) that passes a tag — e.g. to filter or attribute log lines — receives output identical to not passing it, and cannot distinguish "tagged" from "untagged". There is no in-repo caller yet, but this is an exported public contract whose promise (tag appears in the emitted data a caller receives) the body does not implement; per review policy that is a present defect, not a future-caller concern. The parameter also cannot be a harmless no-op by design, since its only possible consumer is the emitted line, which never includes it.

findings.title: Log() accepts tag parameter but body ignores it entirely
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol Log(message string, tag ...string) is a contract carrier whose signature promises a caller may supply a tag for the log entry. The body remains `println(message)` — the tag is never read, formatted, or emitted, and no error/warning is produced. Any caller who passes a tag (e.g. logger.Log("deploy", "prod")) gets output identical to not passing one: the caller's data and intent are silently discarded with no signal. This is the entire change in the PR: either tagged logging was meant to be implemented (and is missing) or the variadic parameter does nothing and should not be added. Accept-and-discard is not a valid contract for a public API, and there is no in-repo caller yet to mask it — the defect ships in the signature itself.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in canDeleteRecord authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting real values: session={isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'}, record={tenantId:'B'} → base returned false (admin AND tenant match), head returns true. The admin arm now requires no tenant match, so an admin of tenant A is authorized to delete records of tenant B — tenant isolation is broken. Second substitution: session={isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'}, record={tenantId:'A', ownerId:'someone-else'} → head returns true, so any non-admin user of a tenant is authorized to delete ANY record in that tenant; RecordRef.ownerId is never compared, and the base policy required admin, so this is a privilege escalation on every record in the tenant. Both arms of the OR widen the authorized set; the function exists solely as a delete gate, so its return value is the authorization decision — unauthorized delete equates to data loss.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now allows non-admin and cross-tenant deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting values: session={isAdmin:false, tenantId:'t1'}, record={tenantId:'t1', ownerId:'u2'} → base evaluated false && true = false (denied); head evaluates false || true = true (allowed). The change has two widening effects: (1) isAdmin no longer gates anything for same-tenant sessions, so any regular user of a tenant can delete any record in it, including other users' records — RecordRef.ownerId is never considered; (2) an admin of one tenant can now delete records in any other tenant, breaking the tenant-scoping the base version enforced. This function is the module's only authorization predicate, so every delete flow built on it inherits both escapes.

findings.title: AND→OR flips delete authorization: non-admins and cross-tenant admins now granted
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting the changed predicate: {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} vs record in tenant 'B' — base: false (rejected), head: true (granted): an admin can now delete records in ANY tenant, breaking tenant isolation. {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} vs record in tenant 'A' — base: false, head: true: any non-admin tenant member can now delete any record in the tenant, including other users' records (ownerId is never consulted). The new predicate is true for every session except non-admins from another tenant — i.e. the admin-only, tenant-scoped gate the base code enforced is inverted, on the only permission check in the codebase, guarding a destructive (data-loss) operation. A flip of a boolean connective in an exported authorization predicate with no test, doc, or comment asserting a deliberate policy change reads as a typo-class regression, not an intentional policy; if cross-tenant admin deletion were intended, the tenant-scope check would still need to remain for non-admins.

findings.title: Swallowed parse errors cause settings to be overwritten with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch routes EVERY failure — JSON.parse error (line 10), 'bad theme' (line 11), 'bad fontSize' (line 12) — into `return { ...DEFAULTS }` (line 15) instead of propagating an exception. The error signal that previously reached callers is gone, and the fallback is indistinguishable from a legitimate settings object. On the only in-repo path, updateFontSize (lines 19-23) calls parseSettings (line 20) and unconditionally persists it via save(JSON.stringify(settings)) (line 22). Before this PR, invalid raw (e.g. truncated file, old-format or partially-invalid blob such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"ten"}) made parseSettings throw, so updateFontSize never called save and the persisted file stayed intact for manual recovery. After this PR, updateFontSize saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} back over the invalid blob, silently destroying any still-valid fields (theme: "dark" is lost) and clobbering the file. No log, no error, no distinction between 'settings loaded' and 'settings were bad and got replaced with defaults'.

findings.title: parseSettings swallow-all catch silently overwrites settings via updateFontSize
findings.whyItBreaks: The added catch is inside the same try block as the explicit validation throws ('bad theme' at line 11, 'bad fontSize' at line 12), so those guards are now dead code: any error — a JSON syntax error OR a wrong-type field — is mapped to DEFAULTS with no log. Concretely, updateFontSize (line 20) calls parseSettings, sets fontSize, and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22. With realistic corrupt input such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"} (a string fontSize, exactly the case line 12 was written to reject), base behavior propagated 'bad fontSize' and save() was never called, preserving the original data for repair/migration. Head behavior silently returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14}, mutates it, and persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, permanently destroying the user's theme 'dark' — failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate default settings object, so the persistence layer cannot tell the fallback from real data. parseSettings is an exported public path; every eventual consumer is forced to conflate failure with a value.

findings.title: Silent default fallback persists over settings file, swallows errors
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings previously threw on invalid JSON or wrong-typed fields; now the bare catch{} swallows both JSON.parse failures and the explicit validation throws (lines 11-12) and returns { theme:'light', fontSize:14 }. Error is not logged and the fallback is indistinguishable from a legitimately configured defaults value. Worse, the only in-repo consumer updateFontSize (lines 20-22) calls parseSettings and then unconditionally calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) — previously any corrupt/invalid raw (e.g. {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"oops"} or a truncated file) made it throw BEFORE save, leaving the user's file intact; now the corrupt file is silently overwritten with {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, destroying recoverable fields (theme) with zero signal to the caller. Both functions are exported public API, so every external caller is forced to conflate 'settings corrupt' with 'user saved defaults', and the save() callback cannot tell it is persisting a fabricated value.

findings.title: pageCount floor drops remainder items from result
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount(totalItems, pageSize) promises the number of pages covering all items; the body was changed from Math.ceil to Math.floor. Substitution: pageCount(25, 10) returns 2, but 25 items at 10 per page require 3 pages. Any consumer iterating pages 0..pageCount-1 (i.e. for (let p = 0; p < pageCount(n, s); p++) ...) never renders items 20-24 — the last partial page is unreachable, so those records are silently lost from every user's view for any totalItems not divisible by pageSize. No doc, signature, or name change accompanies the body change, so the contract 'count of pages covering all items' is unchanged; ceil is the only correct implementation. The base version (Math.ceil) was correct; nothing in the diff justifies the inversion.

findings.title: buildReport artifacts decoupled from builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code derived both fields from one commit: artifactsAt(ref(branch)) is exactly the commit recorded in builtFrom (git show e42e802:src/report.ts:12-13). Head fetches artifacts from ref('verified') — a hardcoded ref name with no definition, constant, or usage anywhere in the repo (rg 'verified' finds only this line). When the 'verified' ref resolves to a different commit than the branch (the norm for a promoted/verified build), the exported BuildReport pairs builtFrom=<branch commit> with artifacts belonging to a different commit, and nothing in the contract (BuildReport's 'artifacts' field has no attribution other than builtFrom) or docs signals the divergence. The branch parameter now governs only builtFrom: buildReport(build, 'main') and buildReport(build, 'release') return the same artifacts. If ref('verified') returns a sentinel/empty value for an undefined ref, artifactsAt(sentinel) silently yields an empty/wrong list for a real build. Every caller of this public function receives a self-inconsistent report.

findings.title: buildReport mixes branch ref and hardcoded 'verified' ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior (f3126a2) returned artifacts at the same commit as builtFrom. The new code resolves 'builtFrom' from build.ref(branch) but fetches artifacts via build.ref('verified'), a hardcoded ref unrelated to the branch argument. For any branch whose ref differs from the 'verified' ref — which is exactly why the branch parameter exists — the returned BuildReport describes two different commits: a consumer deploying or recording artifacts from this report misattributes them to the builtFrom commit, and the branch parameter no longer influences artifacts at all. The change also silently drops the base invariant that artifacts correspond to builtFrom.

findings.title: buildReport returns artifacts from 'verified' ref but builtFrom from branch ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code guaranteed artifacts and builtFrom came from the same commit (build.artifactsAt(commit)). The change fetches artifacts via build.ref("verified") while builtFrom stays build.ref(branch). Nothing in the Build interface or the function links the two refs, so whenever the verified commit differs from the branch tip (the normal case when the tip is not yet verified), the exported BuildReport silently attributes artifacts to a commit they were not built from — builtFrom is a lie about the artifacts. Consumers using builtFrom to label, archive, or display the artifacts get wrong attribution. The public interface BuildReport { builtFrom: string; artifacts: string[] } carries no way to express that they come from different commits, so no caller can detect the mismatch.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores positive limit, returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor removed `slice(0, limit)` and returns `sorted` (the entire reversed array) whenever limit > 0, while the unchanged doc comment still promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries'. Every caller asking for N entries now silently receives all entries. The only in-repo caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-11), allocates `new Array<string>(20)` and then copies `page.length` items into it; when all.length > 20, `out[i] = page[i]` writes past slot 19 and the returned array grows beyond 20 entries — the feed's size cap is silently broken. The `limit <= 0` guard returns [] as if the fix were intentional, but for positive limits the parameter is now dead.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps output at limit — returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;` — for any `limit >= 1` the `.slice(0, limit)` cap is gone, so the function returns every entry. This violates the unchanged doc promise 'Returns at most `limit` entries' (TRIGGER C: public exported carrier, promise=cap, body=no cap). It also breaks the live in-repo caller: renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and then fills `const out = new Array<string>(20)` with `out[i] = page[i]` for `i < page.length`. With the cap removed, `page.length` equals `all.length` (e.g. 2000 feed items), the assignments extend the array past index 19, and renderFeed now returns the full unbounded feed instead of at most 20 entries — a direct regression from base behavior where `page.length <= 20` was guaranteed by the slice. The `limit <= 0 → []` guard is a separate, benign addition (limit=0 also yielded [] under the old slice; no caller passes non-positive limits), but it does not compensate for the dropped positive-limit cap.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit: returns full array instead of capped
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removed `slice(0, limit)` and replaced it with `if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;` (src/feed.ts:4-5). For every limit > 0, the function now returns the entire (reversed) input, violating the unchanged doc promise 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.' (src/feed.ts:1) and the `limit` parameter contract of this exported API. The in-repo consumer renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) (src/feed.ts:9) and writes page[i] for i < page.length into `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10-11); when the feed exceeds 20 entries, the loop writes at indices >= 20, and JS auto-extends the array, so renderFeed also returns the full feed instead of a 20-entry page — a direct user-visible regression on the exported path, plus unbounded returns for any library consumer that relied on the cap for pagination/memory bounds.

findings.title: header entry-count ignores stale filter, mismatches rows
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now renders rows only for non-stale entries, but line 22 still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length). The emitted '# entry-count: N' is computed over the unfiltered array, so when any entry has stale=true the header declares N entries while the body contains fewer rows. The count is part of the export manifest's public output contract — any consumer parsing entry-count to size, verify, or enumerate the manifest will see a declared count that does not match the rows. The mismatch is introduced by this diff: at base, rows came from the same unfiltered array as the count, so header and body always agreed.

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries excluded from rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries out of the emitted rows (line 20-21) but the header still receives the unfiltered length: `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` at line 22. When any entry has stale=true, the manifest advertises `# entry-count: N` where N > actual row count, with no marker identifying which entries were omitted. The count is a machine-readable contract of the generated manifest: any downstream consumer that sizes buffers, displays "N files", or validates row count against the header receives a wrong value or fails a consistency check. Before this PR the header always matched the rows; after it, every manifest containing at least one stale entry is internally inconsistent. The stale entries are also silently dropped with no indication in the output. Fix: pass the filtered length so header and rows always agree: `headerLines(opts, live.length)`.

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries excluded from rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `live` filter removes `stale` entries from `rows`, but the header is still rendered with `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` (line 22, unchanged) which passes the FULL count including stale entries. Base behavior was consistent (rows == entries.length); this diff makes header and body diverge whenever any entry is stale. The `# entry-count: N` comment is an output-format contract of the exported `renderManifest`: a consumer that parses the header to preallocate, loop N times, or verify completeness now receives an over-count and mis-reads/truncates the manifest body. Minimal fix: pass `live.length` to headerLines so the reported count matches the emitted rows (or document/rename the field if the total is intentional — currently nothing distinguishes the two).

findings.title: execute() now always throws, breaking its exported contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `execute(input: string): string` promises that a string is returned for any input; the only body line now throws unconditionally with no branch on input. The prior behavior (returning input.toUpperCase()) was the sole functional path of the module and is fully removed with no replacement. Any consumer — now or in the future — calling this public function gets an exception on the first invocation instead of a string, and the return type annotation actively misleads callers into assuming a value is produced. A public signature promising a result the body never delivers is a contract defect: callers cannot even distinguish failure from a value since failure is the only outcome.

findings.whyItBreaks: `execute` is the only exported function of this module and its signature `execute(input: string): string` still promises a string result, but the body was replaced with `throw new Error("always fails")`. The function never returns: every caller — this PR's own consumers of src/runner.ts at any call site — receives an unconditional exception instead of the uppercased string, and the previous behavior (return input.toUpperCase()) is silently removed with no replacement implementation. This is a complete functional regression of the module: it cannot produce any value anymore. The changed line itself is the defect; even though no callers exist in-repo, an exported public carrier whose promised value is never delivered breaks every downstream consumer at runtime.

findings.title: execute() always throws; exported API can never return a value
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return input.toUpperCase();` with `throw new Error("always fails");`. The public signature `execute(input: string): string` promises a string return for any string input; the body now throws unconditionally, so no call can succeed. Every consumer of this exported function (the module's sole export) crashes on the first call, and the previous correct behavior (uppercasing) is unreachable — not merely conditional, but impossible by construction. This also breaks the contract promised by the unchanged return-type annotation (TRIGGER C): body no longer implements the declared behavior.

findings.title: Viewer gate makes read-only branch unreachable; viewers now rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is read at exactly one place: handle() @ src/handler.ts:24. Callers of handle() pass viewer requests: the same function contains a dedicated dispatch branch `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only"` @ src/handler.ts:25, evidencing viewers were intended to be processed (not rejected). Before this PR, {status:'active', role:'viewer', attempts:1} was eligible → handle returned "read-only". After this PR, isEligible returns false for the same input → handle returns "rejected", and the "read-only" branch at line 25 is now dead code that can never execute. Either the gate is wrong (viewers should get read-only) or the branch is stale (viewers should be rejected); the PR ships both at once, so every viewer request gets a different outcome than the still-present read-only contract promises. The other two checks in isEligible (status, attempts) concern request state; mixing role authorization into this state-predicate silently narrows the meaning of the exported isEligible contract for all callers.

findings.title: Viewer guard over-blocks handle's read-only outcome
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` to isEligible, but the sole consumer, handle() (line 24), has its own explicit viewer branch at line 25 that returns "read-only". findings.title: Payment gate blocks saving unpaid drafts

The added `&& order.payment === "paid"` conjunct is legitimate for submit (blocking submission of unpaid orders), but saveDraft is a draft-persistence action whose legitimacy is independent of the payment gate: an order in the canonical {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} combination was saveable at base and is now rejected. Substituting the value: canProceed({state:"draft",payment:"missing"}) = ("draft" !== "ready") && ("missing" === "paid") = true && false = false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved" at src/actions.ts:9. Because drafts are exactly the state where payment may still be missing, this freezes the primary draft workflow and there is no other path in the repo that would unblock it.

findings.title: dbg! moves items; next line fails to compile (E0382)
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` expands (std, stable since 1.32) to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which matches `items` BY VALUE. `Vec<String>` is not Copy, so `dbg!(items);` moves `items` into the match; the statement's result (`tmp`) is then dropped at the `;`, consuming the vector. The very next line, `let total = items.len();`, reads a moved-from variable and triggers compiler error E0382 "use of moved value: `items`", so the crate fails to build. Even with the move fixed (`dbg!(&items)`), `dbg!` is not gated on debug_assertions and would print every item to stderr on each call in release builds too — a leftover debug artifact with production output side effects.

findings.title: Remove leftover dbg! that dumps all items to stderr in every build

On every call to the public `process` function it formats the entire `items` vec via `Debug` and writes `[src/store.rs:2] items = [...]` to stderr. This is an O(n) formatting + I/O regression on a lib function that previously had zero side effects, pollutes service logs with the full contents of data passed to a store (which may include sensitive user-supplied values), and adds unbounded overhead if `process` is called per item or per request. Verified: `dbg!(items)` expands to a block that returns the value, so `items.len()` on the next line still compiles — no compile error masks it.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items; items.len() is use-after-move, build broken
findings.whyItBreaks: The `dbg!` macro expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }` — it takes its argument BY VALUE and returns it. In a statement `dbg!(items);` the returned Vec<String> is discarded and dropped at the statement's end, so `items` is moved away. The very next line, `let total = items.len();`, borrows `items` again. Vec<String> is not Copy, so this is error[E0382] use of moved value — the crate fails to compile and the public `process` is unusable by any caller. findings.title: changedPaths computed against latest, not pinned tag
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface explicitly documents (lines 7-8, unchanged): fromRevision is "the revision the changed paths were computed against" and "consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." The base version honored this by passing `from` (= resolve(pinnedTag)) to readChangedPaths. The PR adds `const latest = store.resolve("latest")` (line 15) and passes `latest` instead (line 18) while still returning fromRevision = `from` (line 17). Whenever resolve(pinnedTag) != resolve("latest") — the entire purpose of a pinned tag is to differ from a moving "latest" — the returned pair is self-inconsistent: a consumer replaying the changeset on top of fromRevision applies a path set computed against a different base, either shipping wrong/extra paths or silently dropping all changes since the pin (worst case readChangedPaths(latest) yields the empty/newer-than-tip set). The pin's effect on changedPaths is silently discarded. Both fields are exported public API and there is no in-repo caller to mask the inconsistency, so the defect ships now.

findings.title: buildChangeset computes changedPaths against 'latest', not fromRevision base

The diff leaves fromRevision = store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 14) but changes changedPaths to store.readChangedPaths(latest) (line 18) with latest = store.resolve('latest') (line 15). For any caller that pins a tag other than 'latest' — the normal use of a pinnedTag — the returned changeset is internally inconsistent: its paths are relative to the 'latest' commit while fromRevision points at the pinned commit. A consumer that replays the change list on top of fromRevision will either apply patches against the wrong base (garbled/incorrect patch application) or, if 'latest' resolves to the store tip, readChangedPaths(latest) yields the HEAD..HEAD diff (empty or pathless), silently dropping every changed path from the release while fromRevision still advertises a non-empty base — a silent data-loss path. There is no code path where using 'latest' is justified: 'from' is already the intended diff base, and 'latest' is merely a second resolution that can also throw for stores that have no such tag (a new crash point that did not exist before).

findings.title: changedPaths computed against "latest" while fromRevision stays pinned
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported interface documents that fromRevision is "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision" (lines 6-8). The change adds `latest = store.resolve("latest")` and calls `store.readChangedPaths(latest)`, so the object now reports `fromRevision` = the *pinned* tag while `changedPaths` was diffed against `latest`. Whenever `resolve(pinnedTag) != resolve("latest")` — the normal case for a pin, since the whole reason to pass a pinnedTag is to select a revision other than the newest — every consumer that replays the changeset on top of `fromRevision` (as documented) gets a diff set that omits all paths changed between the pin and latest, and includes paths from after latest. Applying a diff computed against a newer tree onto the pinned revision will misapply or fail. The strict-replay contract is now internally contradictory; the two fields must share one base revision.

The helper's explicit None return path is now unconditionally unhandled in its only consumer.

findings.title: Missing config file now crashes startup() with bare TypeError
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() is explicitly designed to return None when the settings file does not exist (line 5-7: `if not os.path.exists(path): return None`). Before this diff, startup() handled that designed input by substituting {"workers": 1, ...} and returning 1. After the diff, the None case falls through to `settings["workers"]`, which raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` — a crash that gives no hint that the cause is a missing config file. If the intent was to make a missing config fatal, the failure should be an explicit, describeable error (e.g., FileNotFoundError naming the path); if the intent was to keep the tolerant behavior, this is a direct regression. Either way, the deletion replaces the only handling of an explicitly-produced None return with an unhandled wrong-typed exception, and no in-repo caller or test in the current tree indicates the missing-file path no longer occurs.

findings.title: Charge swallows submit error and returns nil on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)` followed by `return nil`. Charge's error return is the only failure signal a caller has: before the change, a non-nil error unambiguously meant 'the gateway did not accept the charge'; after the change, Charge returns nil both when Submit succeeds AND when Submit fails (only the invalid-amount guard still returns non-nil). Any caller that gates persistence/billing/order state on `err == nil` will record a failed payment as paid (false success), or skip retry/refund logic. This is an exported public function (capital C), and the log line is not a substitute: the error never reaches the caller, so failure and legitimate nil are indistinguishable at every decision point. Trigger D fires: signal=gw.Submit error, previously_reached=caller via wrapped return (old line 14), now_receives=nil.

findings.title: Charge returns nil when gateway Submit fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaced `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)` + fall-through to `return nil`. The error signal from gw.Submit is discarded: Charge (exported, package pay) now returns a nil error on gateway failure, identical to the success return value. Any caller — e.g. a checkout handler that fulfills an order or records a charge as paid when err == nil — cannot distinguish 'gateway declined/failed' from 'charged', so a failed charge is acted on as success (goods shipped/order marked paid without payment). The wrapped `%w` chain is also downgraded to `%v`, losing errors.Is/errors.As capability. The contract is also internally incoherent: the invalid-amount branch (line 14) still returns an error, but the failure path that actually matters no longer does. The public signature `Charge(...) error` promises error-on-failure; swallowing is not part of any stated contract.

findings.title: Charge swallows Submit error and returns nil on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version propagated the gateway failure (`return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)`, base pay/charge.go:14), so callers could distinguish a failed charge from a successful one. The head version replaces that with `log.Printf("charge failed: %v", err)` and falls through to `return nil`. Charge's exported contract — non-nil error means the charge did not go through — is now broken: every caller (current or future) is forced to treat a failed charge as success, and the only remaining signal is an unstructured log line. Any caller that checks the error to decide whether money was captured, retry the submission, or reconcile will act on the failure as if it were a real success. This is a payment path; the fallback is not part of any documented contract — it silently degrades failure to success.

findings.title: cache key drops tenantId: cross-tenant settings leak
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) builds 'settings:'+name with no tenantId, and settingsFor uses it at line 12. The store contract (fetch(tenantId, name)) is per-tenant, but the cache is now global. Substitution: settingsFor('A','theme',s) misses, fetches A's value, sets cache['settings:theme']=vA. settingsFor('B','theme',s) then hits cache['settings:theme'] and returns vA to tenant B without ever calling store.fetch('B','theme'). Any two tenants that read the same setting name collide, so tenant B silently receives tenant A's value — wrong behavior plus cross-tenant disclosure of possibly sensitive settings. invalidate(name) at lines 20-21 is consistent with the broken key but its signature change (dropping tenantId) also means a single invalidate clears the shared entry for every tenant; if a caller still passes the old two arguments it would delete key 'settings:<tenantId>' and fail to invalidate the real entry.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still takes tenantId and calls store.fetch(tenantId, name) (line 15) — per-tenant semantics are the contract, and SettingsStore.fetch is scoped by tenant. But the cache key is now cacheKey(name) = `settings:${name}` only (lines 7-9, 12), and the module-level Map is shared across all tenants. Concrete failure: settingsFor('tenantA','flag',storeA) populates cache under `settings:flag`; settingsFor('tenantB','flag',storeB) hits at line 13-14 and returns tenantA's value without ever calling storeB.fetch. Every tenant sharing a setting name receives the first tenant's cached value — wrong tenant configuration served, and if settings carry tenant-specific secrets/flags this is a tenant-isolation breach. The base version keyed by `${tenantId}:${name}`, so this is a regression introduced here. The invalidate signature change (lines 20-21) shares the root cause: invalidation is no longer tenant-scoped, and any existing caller of invalidate(tenantId, name) silently deletes `settings:${tenantId}` — a no-op that leaves the stale cross-tenant entry in place indefinitely, so a settings update never propagates for other tenants.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenantId: cross-tenant settings leak
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code keyed the cache as `${tenantId}:${name}`; this PR replaces it with `cacheKey(name)` = `settings:${name}`, dropping tenantId entirely. But settingsFor still fetches via the tenant-scoped store.fetch(tenantId, name) (SettingsStore interface, line 2), so the cache key no longer matches the fetch's tenant dimension. Concrete live path: settingsFor('tenantA','theme') misses, fetches A's value, caches under settings:theme. settingsFor('tenantB','theme') then hits the same key and returns tenant A's value — tenant B's fetch is never called and tenant B receives tenant A's settings (feature flags, branding, config). The last writer wins for every tenant. The same defect hits invalidate (lines 20-21): it now deletes the shared tenant-agnostic key, so one tenant's invalidation clears every tenant's entry, and there is no way to invalidate a single tenant — while the exported signature change (removed tenantId param) also breaks any existing TypeScript caller at compile time and silently wrong-keys JavaScript callers.

findings.title: reserve() check-then-act race oversells stock after async conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads remaining and evaluates `remaining <= 0` BEFORE `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) but writes the decremented count AFTER it (line 18). await suspends the async function, so two overlapping calls for the same sku (e.g. fire-and-forget `reserve('A'); reserve('A');` or two concurrent requests) both read remaining=1, both pass the guard, both save 0, both set 0 and both return true — one unit of stock grants two reservations. The sync base version was atomic within an event-loop tick; the diff inserts the suspension point. The persisted value is also computed from the same stale read, so the durable count confirms the oversell.

findings.title: async reserve() check-then-act race oversells last unit
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff moves the stock update behind an `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17), so the read/guard at lines 15-16 and the write at line 18 are no longer atomic. Two concurrent reserve('A') calls both read `remaining = 1` before either executes line 18's `stock.set`, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both persist save('A', 0), and both return true — two reservations granted for one unit. The base version was fully synchronous and could not interleave, so this is a regression. Before the await, substitutions: call1 remaining=1 → guard passes → save; call2 remaining=1 → guard passes → save; both true. Outcome: total grants (2) > stock (1).

findings.title: Breaking public API: required Store arg + sync→Promise reserve
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Inventory class gains `constructor(private store: Store)` with no default, and reserve() changes from `boolean` to `Promise<boolean>`. Existing consumers of the base version break in two concrete ways: (1) `new Inventory()` no longer compiles, and if a caller constructs it anyway, `this.store` is undefined so the success path throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'save')` at line 17 — an uncaught exception where the base version never threw; (2) old-style callers that use the return value synchronously (`if (inventory.reserve(sku))` / `const ok = reserve(sku)`) now read a Promise object, which is always truthy — reservation is reported as success even when remaining <= 0 returned false, and a save rejection becomes a floating unhandled rejection since nothing in the call path awaits. Base version has no callers updated in this diff (repo contains only src/inventory.ts).

findings.title: async reserve breaks atomicity: concurrent calls can double-reserve
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version was a synchronous read-check-write (atomic in single-threaded JS). The head version reads `remaining` (line 15), checks the guard, then `await`s `store.save` (line 17) BEFORE writing the map (line 18). Two concurrent calls for the same sku (e.g. two request handlers, or `Promise.all([reserve(sku), reserve(sku)])` while stock=1) both read `remaining=1`, both pass `remaining <= 0`, both persist `remaining-1=0` and both return `true` — 1 unit is double-reserved and the store records 0 while both callers believe they hold a reservation. In the base code this interleaving was impossible because no await separated the read from the write. The sold-out check `remaining <= 0` is now a stale-check-and-late-write: the guard can no longer prevent two in-flight reservations of the last unit.

findings.title: retry() still multiplies backoff by 1000 after unit change to ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() switched from seconds (min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (min(30000, 2**attempt * 1000)), and schedulePoll was updated to stop multiplying by 1000. But the third consumer, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. Pre-change: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, capped 30s per attempt. Post-change the same line sleeps 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, and then 30,000,000 ms (8.3 HOURS) per attempt once the cap kicks in — a=2 already waits 66 minutes, a=3 waits 2.2h. Any retry() loop with attempts >= 3 effectively hangs for hours to days instead of retrying within seconds, blocking whatever job awaited it.

findings.title: Retry backoff now sleeps 1000x too long (16min to 8.3h)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)); this PR redefines it to return milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and correctly dropped the '*1000' in poll.ts. But the second and only other consumer, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)` — now multiplying milliseconds by 1000. Verified arithmetic: attempt 0 sleeps 1,000,000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1s; attempt 1 ~33 min; attempts >=5 hit the 30,000ms cap and sleep 30,000,000ms (~8.3 hours) instead of 30s. A single transient failure in the retry loop now stalls the job for 16 minutes at minimum and hours at the cap, effectively hanging the retry path (an exported public API: export async function retry). The unit change to a shared helper with one call site left on the old unit is the defect.

findings.title: backoff() unit change breaks retry.ts: sleeps are 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from returning seconds to returning milliseconds, but only poll.ts was updated. The unchanged consumer src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, so every retry delay is multiplied by 1000: attempt 0 now sleeps 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1,000 ms; at the cap (attempt >= 5) each retry sleeps 30,000 * 1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. A 5-attempt retry now blocks ~8.6 h instead of ~61 s, effectively hanging the retry workflow. The migration must also remove the `* 1000` at retry.ts:12 (or backoff must keep returning seconds).

findings.title: Return f.Close() error instead of discarding it via defer
findings.whyItBreaks: w.Flush() only moves bufio's buffer into the kernel page cache; os.File.Close on a write-mode file is the point where write-back failures surface (EIO, ENOSPC on delayed-allocation/NFS/network filesystems). The old code propagated that signal via 'return f.Close()' (@base line 20). The new code 'return w.Flush()' (line 20) plus ignored 'defer f.Close()' (line 13) makes Save return nil even when the data was never durably written — a silent data-loss signal. Save is an exported function (package store), so every caller (currently none in-repo, but this is the persistence entry point) unconditionally conflates close failure with success. The loop/flush error paths are unaffected: those already discarded f.Close() before the change.

findings.title: Save() silently discards f.Close() error after refactor
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code returned f.Close()'s error ('return f.Close()'), so a close-time failure (delayed write-back errors, NFS commit failures, EIO on close, quota/ENOSPC surfaced at close) reached the caller as a non-nil error. New code uses 'defer f.Close()' (line 13) whose return value is discarded, and returns only w.Flush() (line 20). If Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save returns nil while the data may not be durably persisted — the caller cannot distinguish success from a failed write and may report/act on the save as successful. Save is an exported public function, so this degraded contract is shipped now even without in-repo callers.

findings.title: Save() swallows file Close error on success path
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D. Base code returned `f.Close()` (previous line 24: `return f.Close()`), so a close-time write-back failure (e.g. delayed-allocation flush error on NFS/network filesystems, EIO surfacing at close) propagated to every caller as a non-nil error. Head code does `defer f.Close()` (line 13) and `return w.Flush()` (line 20): the deferred Close's error is discarded, so after `w.Flush()` succeeds but `f.Close()` fails, Save() returns nil. Since Save is exported, every caller is forced to conflate 'close failed / data not durable' with 'saved successfully' — a caller persisting data (e.g. config/state file) on Save()==nil can report success and lose data. The error is not logged and not distinguishable at any decision point; the contract change is a regression from the base code which deliberately propagated it.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of each page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: The new loop is `for position in range(start, end - 1)`, but _window_bounds (line 17-21, docstring line 18: "Half-open [start, end) bounds") returns a half-open end. The old code used `range(start, end)` (base commit 05b495e, lib/pagination.py:19) and included the page's last row. Now, for rows=[a,b,c,d], page_size=3: page 0 has start=0, end=3, so range(0,2) yields only rows 0,1 — row 'c' is never collected; page 1 has start=3, end=4, so range(3,3) is empty — row 'd' is never collected. Every page silently loses its final row; the whole dataset's last row is always lost; a single-row page (start=0, end=1, range(0,0)) renders an empty string. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) both inherit the loss, so rendered output omits rows that the base version included.

findings.title: page_window off-by-one drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite changed the window loop from the base version's `range(start, end)` to `range(start, end - 1)`, while _window_bounds still returns the standard half-open [start, end) bounds (docstring line 18 confirms). Substituting real values: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → page 0: start=0, end=2, range(0,1) returns ['a'] ('b' lost); page 1: start=2, end=4, range(2,3) returns ['c'] ('d' lost); page 2: start=4, end=5, range(4,4) returns [] ('e' lost entirely). Every page with >=2 rows loses its last element, and the final row of the list never appears in any output. page_window is a public function and the sole data source for render_page and summarize (lines 40, 52), so both silently produce incomplete output — a silent data-loss regression versus base, which returned the full page.

findings.title: page_window off-by-one drops last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: `_window_bounds` at line 18 documents and returns half-open [start, end) bounds, but the loop uses `range(start, end - 1)`, which yields [start, end-1) and skips index end-1. Substituting real values: page_window(range(10), 0, 3) -> [0,1] (base commit returned [0,1,2]); the final page of 10 rows (page 3: start=9, end=10) -> range(9,9) -> [] (row 9 lost); page_window(['x'], 0, 3) -> [] (was ['x']). Via render_page/summarize, rows 2,5,8,9 of a 10-row/3-per-page summary are silently omitted and numbering jumps 1,2,4,5,7,8 — the public API of this module now mis-renders every dataset whose last page has fewer than 2 rows or whose pages contain more than 1 row.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired values and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Substitute a normal hit: entry stored 1ms ago, ttlMs=60000 → age(1) > 60000 is false → control falls to this.entries.delete(key) + return null. So every read of a not-yet-expired entry destroys it and reports a miss — the cache never serves fresh data. Substitute an expired entry: age > ttl is true → the stale value is returned past its TTL and is never deleted (delete only runs on the false branch), so expired data is served forever and the Map grows unboundedly. The base version used '<', which was correct; this is a full inversion of both outcomes, not a boundary fix. TtlCache.get is the exported public contract of the class; its sole purpose is defeated in both directions.

findings.title: pruneDone splice during forward forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Substitute jobs=[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]: forEach index 0 sees a done job and splice(0,1) shifts the array to [{done:true},{done:false}]; forEach then advances to index 1, which is now {done:false} — the second done job is never visited and survives in the returned array. Any two adjacent completed jobs leave a done job in the queue, so the pruner silently under-counts on a common shape (batch of consecutive completed jobs). Additionally, the old body returned jobs.filter(...), a new array that left the caller's input untouched; splice mutates the caller's array in place, so a caller keeping a reference to the original array sees silent modification where it previously had immutability.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check returns expired values, deletes fresh entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from '<' to '>'. age = Date.now() - entry.storedAt; age > ttlMs now means EXPIRED, yet the code returns entry.value — so callers receive stale data past its TTL. Conversely, fresh entries (age <= ttlMs) fall through to this.entries.delete(key), evicting the entry on the first read within TTL; every subsequent get returns null, so the cache stops caching. Base code ('<') had correct semantics; this is a full inversion of the public TtlCache.get contract.

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips elements, leaving done jobs in queue
findings.whyItBreaks: jobs.splice(index, 1) shifts all later elements left by one while forEach's index advances to index+1, so the element that shifted into the current position is never re-examined. For runs of adjacent done jobs, survivors remain: [done,done] → [done]; [done,done,done,done] → [done,done]; [done,done,pending] → [done,pending]. pruneDone therefore returns a queue that still contains done jobs — any downstream drain/dispatch of the returned array will process already-completed jobs. Additionally, the base implementation (jobs.filter) returned a new array without touching the input; the new code mutates the caller's array in place, so other holders of the original reference observe a partially-pruned, order-shifted array.

findings.title: TtlCache TTL comparison inverted: expired served, fresh entries deleted
findings.whyItBreaks: The operator changed from `<` (base: return value while age < ttl, else delete) to `>` (head). Every get() is now wrong: an entry whose age is within TTL (Date.now() - storedAt <= ttl) takes the delete branch and returns null — a guaranteed miss right after set(), so the cache never serves anything fresh. Conversely, an entry whose age exceeds ttl returns its value — stale data is served long past its TTL. Additionally, the delete branch now only runs for fresh entries, so expired entries are never reaped and `entries` grows without bound. Both behaviors are inverted from the class contract.

findings.title: pruneDone splices inside forEach, skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: splice(index,1) shifts every later element left by one, but forEach still advances to index+1, so the element that moved into the vacated index is never visited. Traceable with the exact code: [done,done] -> at index 0 splice removes jobs[0], forEach advances to index 1 while length is now 1 -> loop ends -> returns [done]; [notdone,done,done] -> index 1 splices jobs[1] -> returns [notdone,done]. Any run of two or more consecutive done jobs leaves a done job in the returned array, violating the function's contract (pruneDone must return only unfinished jobs); a consumer looping over the result would re-process already-completed work. It also mutates the caller's array in place, unlike the previous filter semantics.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`, so averageAmount([]) computes 0 / 0 = NaN (reduce on empty array returns the seed 0, then dividing by length 0). Base explicitly handled empty input, meaning empty-row callers were supported; they now receive NaN, which poisons any downstream aggregation and serializes to JSON null. This is a public exported function with the empty case previously a defined contract.

findings.title: busiest sorts the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used `[...rows].sort(...)` to keep the input untouched; head calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, which reorders the caller's array as a side effect. Any caller that reuses `rows` (e.g. for other aggregations, UI ordering, or passing a shared/shared-state array) sees its order destroyed after calling busiest, even though the function only promises to return the max row. The mutation is deterministic on a live path for every caller of this exported function.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows; remove guard regresses contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. With empty input, total = 0 and rows.length = 0, so the function returns 0/0 = NaN instead of the previous 0. This is an exported function: any caller that can pass an empty list (legitimately, e.g. 'no transactions this month') now receives NaN, and NaN silently poisons downstream math — every comparison (`NaN > threshold`, `NaN === NaN`) is false, so sums/aggregations become NaN or comparisons mis-evaluate with no error raised. The previous behavior (0 for empty) was the function's own explicit contract and is now silently lost.

findings.title: busiest now mutates caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`, dropping the defensive copy. `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so calling `busiest(rows)` permanently reorders the caller's array by amount descending. Any caller that reuses `rows` afterward (e.g. rendering rows in their original/chronological order, or computing a second statistic that depends on order) now sees corrupted data. The base version explicitly copied the array to avoid this — a deliberate guard that this PR removes.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed early return `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was the only thing that guaranteed a defined result for empty input. After the change, `[].reduce((sum, row) => sum + row.amount, 0)` yields 0 and `0 / rows.length` is `0 / 0` = NaN. The exported function previously returned 0 for `averageAmount([])`; the same call now returns NaN. NaN poisons every downstream use: arithmetic comparisons are all false, `JSON.stringify` serializes it as `null`, and display/rendering shows `NaN`. The guard was not redundant — this is a silent behavior regression on a public exported function, not just cleanup.

findings.title: busiest now sorts caller's array in place, mutating input
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)` drops the defensive copy: `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so a call to `busiest(rows)` now permanently reorders the caller's array into descending-amount order (and makes the function impure). Any caller that keeps the array for later use — rendering in original/insertion order, computing more stats, passing it to a second consumer — silently gets reordered data after a read-only-looking query call. Same call, different side effect on the same input: this is the dropped-defensive-copy/in-place-mutation-of-caller-data defect class. The correct minimization here is to keep the copy (`[...rows].sort(...)`); the copy was not pointless.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in score sort (lexicographic ranking)
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units, so scores.reverse() produces lexicographic-descending order, not numeric-descending. Concrete case: players [{a,2},{b,10}], n=1 → sort() gives [10,2], reverse() gives [2,10], cutoff = scores[0] = 2 → topPlayers returns the player with score 2, the LOWEST scorer. The base revision (sort((a,b)=>b-a)) correctly returned the score-10 player. Any input mixing single- and multi-digit scores (e.g. [100,90,12] → sorted [100,12,90] → reversed [90,12,100]) yields a wrong cutoff, so the exported topPlayers and its in-repo consumer formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) both emit wrong rankings.

findings.title: rankScores default sort ranks lexicographically, wrong top players
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units, so scores sort as text, not numbers. [10, 2, 100].sort() = [10, 100, 2]; .reverse() = [2, 100, 10]. topPlayers(players, 2) then uses cutoff = scores[1] = 100, so the score-10 player (2nd highest by any numeric reading) fails the `p.score >= cutoff` filter and is dropped from the result; base code used sort((a,b) => b - a) which was correct. The public export topPlayers (consumed by formatBoard at line 20, which renders the ranked board) therefore returns the wrong set of leaders whenever scores differ in magnitude/digit count (e.g. 100 vs 99 vs 10; also wrong ordering among 2-digit+ values). Also triggers TRIGGER C (contract drift): the unchanged public carrier `topPlayers` promises descending top-n by score while the body computes lexicographic order; the only in-repo caller formatBoard relies on the promise.

findings.title: rankScores default sort() breaks numeric top-N selection
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and compares by UTF-16 code units, not numeric value. Base code used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) (verified via git show 1da2645), which sorted numerically descending. The new code does scores.sort(); scores.reverse(); so e.g. scores [50, 100] sort lexicographically to [100, 50] ("100" < "50"), then reverse to [50, 100]. With n=1, cutoff = scores[0] = 50, so topPlayers([{a,50},{b,100}], 1) filters score >= 50 (both pass) and slice(0,1) returns {a,50} — the LOWEST scorer as top, instead of {b,100}. The bug affects any score set where values differ in digit count (e.g. 9 vs 100, 2 vs 100); it silently happens to work only for single-digit scores. formatBoard (line 20) relies on topPlayers, so the emitted leaderboard is wrong.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison (timing side-channel)
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates handle()'s 401/200 decision, which is the only authentication on the webhook path. The diff replaces hmac.compare_digest with str.__eq__, which short-circuits at the first differing character. An attacker who can observe response timing can recover the valid hmac-sha256 signature one byte at a time (each correct prefix makes the comparison run longer), then forge a signature that passes verify() and reaches processor() with an arbitrary payload. Functionally the comparison still returns the same boolean; only the timing changed, which is exactly why the original used compare_digest. This is a pure weakening of an existing security control with no compensating benefit.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in webhook verify
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature. Python str equality short-circuits at the first mismatching character (and even memcmp-based paths expose per-byte timing), so the comparison time leaks the expected SHA-256 hex digest one byte at a time. verify() is the sole gate on handle() (app/webhook.py:14), which returns 200 and executes processor(payload) on success — an attacker who recovers the digest by timing measurements (e.g. 401 vs 200 latency across many requests against a fixed secret) can forge a valid signature and get attacker-controlled payloads processed. The base code deliberately used compare_digest for exactly this reason; this diff removes that hardening with no compensating control. Accept/reject outcomes for any given input are unchanged (same strings compare equal under both, differing strings unequal), so this is not a correctness change — it is a pure weakening of the security check, and it is not caught by functional tests.

findings.title: Restore constant-time hmac.compare_digest for signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code used hmac.compare_digest, whose entire purpose is constant-time comparison of MACs/signatures. The new `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` is a variable-time string comparison: Python `==` short-circuits at the first differing byte (and lengths differ, it returns immediately). An attacker who controls `given_signature` and measures server response latency on the 401/200 path (handle at app/webhook.py:14-17) can recover the expected digest byte-by-byte, then forge a signature that passes verify() and executes processor(payload) with payload fully attacker-controlled. The boolean outcome of verify() is identical for both implementations for every input, so this change provides no benefit — it only removes the timing-attack mitigation from a security-critical gate.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; transfer no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (68f17b7) all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled back all of them. In head, `db.transaction()` wraps only `_record_ledger` (line 23); commit-on-exit persists the ledger row before `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs. Concrete failures: (1) debit or credit UPDATE raises (CHECK constraint, disk/I-O error) -> ledger already records a transfer that never happened, and the caller gets an exception for a transfer the ledger says succeeded; (2) credit UPDATE fails after the debit UPDATE (itself outside any transaction, so each statement autocommits) -> funds removed from from_acct, never credited to to_acct, ledger says it completed; (3) process crash between line 23 and 24 leaves a committed ledger entry with unchanged balances. Any retry by the caller would double-record the ledger row. This is the exact regression-class this refactor shape produces, and the fix is a one-line move.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; transfer is no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: In base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs shared one transaction: any exception rolled back all three. In head, `_record_ledger` runs inside the `with db.transaction():` block (line 23) and the transaction commits on block exit, then `_apply_balances` (line 24) executes outside any transaction (autocommit). Consequences: (1) If the debit UPDATE at line 10 raises (connection drop, constraint, trigger), the ledger row is already committed — ledger says money moved, balances unchanged; the error propagates, so the caller retries, adding a second ledger row and re-debiting, corrupting the books. (2) If the credit UPDATE at line 14 raises, the debit at line 10 already autocommitted — from_acct is debited, to_acct never credited, ledger committed, no rollback possible. Both failure modes were impossible in the base code, where the same exceptions rolled back everything. The bare `with`/call sequencing is atomicity itself, not refactoring cosmetics.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs were inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled back all three. Head calls `_record_ledger` inside the block but `_apply_balances` AFTER it (line 24), so the ledger row is committed before any balance UPDATE runs. Concrete failure paths: (a) if either UPDATE raises (CHECK(balance>=0), FK, connection loss, disk error), the ledger row for the transfer is already durable while balances are unchanged — the ledger claims a transfer that never happened, and a retry double-records it; (b) if the first UPDATE (debit, line 10-12) autocommits and the second (credit) fails, from_acct is debited, to_acct is never credited, and the ledger records the full transfer — real money loss with an inconsistent audit trail. The exception still propagates to the caller, so this is not a swallowed error — it is a partial-commit/atomicity regression introduced by extracting the helper and placing its call outside the transaction.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time; billing day shifts by host timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The same UTC instant now maps to different date strings depending on the process TZ: verified with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z yields "2024-01-01" before (UTC) but "2023-12-31" after. This is a billing-day classifier, so (1) identical timestamps processed on hosts with different TZ settings (workers, CI, dev vs prod) produce different billing days — non-deterministic bucketing/proration; (2) the in-repo consumer sameBillingDay (line 8) changes result: 01:00Z vs 23:00Z same UTC day now returns false, while 2024-01-01T22:00Z vs 2024-01-02T00:30:00Z (different UTC days) now returns true — day-boundary classification silently flips; (3) any persisted day string or cache key produced under the old UTC contract diverges from recomputed values on upgrade in non-UTC environments. No timezone parameter or policy accompanies the change, so the previous UTC semantics are the contract being broken.

findings.title: billingDay silently changed UTC to local timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version computed the billing day with getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The patch is otherwise a pure refactor (same YYYY-MM-DD format, same padding), so the timezone basis is the only semantic change. For a Date near a midnight boundary the result depends on the machine's TZ: e.g. 2024-01-02T02:30:00Z renders '2024-01-01' when TZ=America/New_York instead of the UTC-based '2024-01-02'. This shifts the billing-day boundary for a billing library, and sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the defect: two instants in the same UTC day now compare unequal (or distinct UTC days compare equal) once local conversion is applied. For two identical instants the output also differs per deployment (server TZ), so persisted/day-keyed comparisons in prior callers break on upgrade.

findings.title: billingDay switched UTC→local time, day key now TZ-dependent
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation built the key from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate (UTC-anchored billing day). The rewrite replaces them with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned 'YYYY-MM-DD' key now depends on the process's local timezone. For the same instant, two hosts with different TZ settings (e.g. TZ=UTC vs TZ=America/New_York) produce different billingDay strings, and any instant near local midnight diverges from the previous output (e.g. new Date('2024-01-01T23:30:00Z') yields '2023-12-31' under TZ=America/New_York but '2024-01-01' under UTC). Callers that compare or persist billingDay keys (sameBillingDay, event/charge bucketing) become host-TZ-dependent and can misclassify the billing day, and existing persisted keys computed under the UTC contract stop matching new ones for the same timestamps. No test, doc, or flag accompanies the change to indicate the UTC contract was intentionally dropped.

findings.title: Cross-tenant cache collision: key must keep tenant prefix
findings.whyItBreaks: memo (src/profile.ts:7) is a module-level singleton shared across all callers, and fetchProfile is explicitly tenant-dependent (src/profile.ts:12,18). With the key reduced to `account` alone: readProfile('tenantA','acct1') fetches and memoizes under 'acct1'; a later readProfile('tenantB','acct1') hits memo.get('acct1') and returns tenantA's Profile (including its `tenant` field) without ever invoking fetchProfile for tenantB. Every tenant with an overlapping account string silently receives another tenant's profile — a deterministic wrong-result/data-leak path, and the miss for tenantB means its profile is never resolved. The previous `${tenant}:${account}` key was correct; this diff removes the tenant disambiguation.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, returning wrong tenant's profile
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a module-level Map shared by all calls to the exported readProfile. The key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`, so any two callers passing the same account string for different tenants collide. Call 1 readProfile('tenantA','acct') fetches and memo.set('acct', profileA); call 2 readProfile('tenantB','acct') hits memo.get('acct') and returns profileA, whose tenant field is 'tenantA', and fetchProfile is never invoked for tenantB. The result is wrong data returned to the caller, with the profile's tenant field mislabeling it for the wrong tenant — a cache-poisoning regression introduced by this diff. The interface (Profile.tenant), the fetch signature (tenant, account), and the previous key all establish tenant as a distinguishing dimension of the profile, so keying on account alone cannot be correct.

findings.title: Memo cache key drops tenant, returning wrong tenant's profile
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is tenant-scoped by contract: fetchProfile takes (tenant, account) and the returned Profile carries a tenant field. The new key `account` (was `${tenant}:${account}`) collides across tenants: after readProfile('tenantA', 'acct1') populates memo['acct1'], any later readProfile('tenantB', 'acct1') hits `if (cached) return cached` and returns tenantA's profile — wrong tenant field, wrong displayName — and tenantB's fetchProfile is never invoked. Base used the tenant-namespaced key precisely to prevent this; the change breaks multi-tenant correctness and profile isolation for an exported public function, with no in-repo evidence that account values are globally unique.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns '' silently
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: ${key}` on an absent key, and loadAll() propagated it. Now the empty catch block converts every absent key (and any exception thrown by store.get) into "" with zero logging. The exported API can no longer distinguish "key absent / store failure" from "key present with empty-string value" — every caller, including loadAll(), is forced to treat failure as real data. Concretely: a caller using load() to read config and then persist/write it back (e.g. sync or merge logic) would persist "" over a real value; a caller branching on truthiness would treat a missing key as an empty-but-present value. The empty catch also swallows errors from store.get itself (any Map subclass or corrupted store), which previously surfaced. Nothing in the repo logs the fallback, so silent data corruption is undetectable.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all converts the deliberately thrown Error(`missing: ${key}`) (line 4) into return "". The error signal no longer reaches any caller: loadAll (src/store.ts:12) previously aborted on a missing key; it now silently produces "" in the result array, so a dropped/missing lookup becomes valid-looking data. Worse, "" is also the legitimate return for a stored empty string (store.get(key) === "" returns at line 5), so failure and a real value are indistinguishable at every consumer. The catch also swallows any error, not only the missing-key case.
