This is an exported public function; the base version's throw-on-missing contract is silently changed with no documentation, and every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns '' silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch turns the deliberate `throw new Error('missing: ' + key)` (line 4) into `return ""` (line 7) with no logging. Empty string is a perfectly valid stored value in Map<string,string>, so any caller (and this is an exported public function) can no longer distinguish 'key absent / failure' from 'key present with empty value'. In-repo, loadAll() (line 12) was the propagation path: previously a missing key aborted the whole batch with an exception; now loadAll returns a successful array containing a fabricated '' at the missing position — silent partial data, indistinguishable from a legitimately empty entry. The catch-all also swallows any future/other error inside the try block. This is a swallowed-failure (TRIGGER D) defect: the fallback is not part of any documented contract, the error is not logged, and the failure value is collision-prone with real data.

findings.title: Make retry and retryBackground share one attempt-count field
findings.whyItBreaks: Config (lines 2-3) now requires BOTH maxAttempts and retries, but retry only reads maxAttempts (line 9) and retryBackground only reads retries (line 22). A config object valid against the exported Config carries one silently ignored field on every call, and the same config yields different attempt budgets depending on which function consumes it. Concrete wrong behavior: a caller migrating an existing `retry(fn, {maxAttempts: 5, timeout: t})` call to `retryBackground` must invent `retries`; setting `retries: 0` (or the common 'retries = extra attempts after the first' convention, e.g. retries:3 meaning 4 total attempts) makes retryBackground invoke fn zero times, silently dropping the operation with no error, while maxAttempts=5 is ignored. retryBackground (lines 20-31) is also a line-for-line duplicate of retry (lines 7-18) differing only in the loop-bound field, so any future fix to one path (deadline check placement, async handling) silently desyncs the other.

findings.title: retryBackground treats retries as total attempts; retries=0 is a silent no-op
findings.whyItBreaks: The new field is NAMED `retries` (contract promise: attempts beyond the first), but the body uses it as the total attempt budget: `for (let i = 0; i < config.retries; i++)`. Substituting the natural config: retries=0 ("no retries" → try once) gives ZERO iterations — fn() is never invoked at all, the function returns void, and the caller sees no error, so it looks like a successful background completion. It also reads a different field than the sibling `retry` (`maxAttempts` @src/retry.ts:9) from the same required `Config`, so a config written for `retry` — e.g. {maxAttempts: 3, retries: 0, timeout: 1000} — passed to retryBackground silently never runs the work. Naming the counter off-by-one means both the "one retry" reading (attempts = retries+1) and the consistent-with-retry reading are unsatisfiable.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows final failure; success and failure are indistinguishable
findings.whyItBreaks: Each attempt's error is discarded by `catch { continue; }` and, once the retry budget is exhausted, the function falls off the end and returns void with no rethrow, no log, and no status. This is a NEW public export: every eventual caller is forced to conflate "all retries failed" with "succeeded" — a background task that failed can never be noticed, surfaced, or compensated. (The pre-existing `retry` shares the pattern, but this PR adds a second public path with the same defect, so it is in scope.)

findings.title: retryBackground counts config.retries while retry counts maxAttempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (lines 20-31) is a line-for-line copy of retry (lines 7-18) except its loop bound reads config.retries (line 22) instead of config.maxAttempts (line 9). The same Config object therefore yields different attempt counts from the two sibling exports: {maxAttempts: 5, retries: 2, timeout: 1000} runs up to 5 iterations in retry but only 2 in retryBackground. Additionally the field name 'retries' conventionally promises attempts after the first, so retries: 2 should allow 3 total attempts, but line 22 executes only 2 total. Config now requires two counters and each function silently honors only one of them; a caller cannot know which knob governs which function. The duplicated body is already diverging.

findings.title: TimeoutMs->timeout rename in exported Config breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Base commit exported Config.timeoutMs (base line 3, used at base line 7); the head renames it to timeout (line 4) with no alias, deprecation, or migration path, and nowhere in the diff requires the rename. Any existing JS/compiled consumer still passing { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } gets config.timeout === undefined, so deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN (lines 8 and 21), and Date.now() > NaN is always false: the deadline guard silently stops firing and retry no longer honors its timeout. The same old config leaves config.retries undefined, so retryBackground's loop (i < undefined, line 22) never executes and fn is silently never invoked. TypeScript consumers fail to compile instead. This is an upgrade breakage of the module's only public contract.

findings.title: Input defaultValue replaced by value length, losing the actual value
findings.whyItBreaks: Base rendered defaultValue={value} — the input contained the value. Head renders defaultValue={'len=' + value.length}, so an input fed value "hello" now contains "len=5" instead of "hello". The Field's only behavior (displaying/editing its value) is destroyed for every existing string caller: the user sees the length, not the value, and a form submission carries the wrong text. Even if displaying the length were intended, it belongs outside the input, not in defaultValue.

findings.title: value widened to string | number but .length is undefined on numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported FieldProps.value is widened from string to string | number, but the body reads value.length. Primitive numbers have no .length (verified: (42).length === undefined), so any number passed renders defaultValue="len=undefined" — the advertised `number` case produces garbage rather than a length. Under standard TS lib this combination is also a compile error ('Property length does not exist on type number'), so the widened type and the body contradict each other. This is a public exported carrier whose promised accepted input type is not implemented (TRIGGER C); the promised behavior affects the rendered data a caller receives.

findings.title: value.length is invalid on string|number union and yields len=undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff widens the exported FieldProps.value from string to string | number, promising numbers are valid input, but the new body reads value.length. TypeScript rejects property access on a union when the property is absent from any member (number has no `length`) — TS2339, so the file no longer typechecks. If compiled with type-stripping only, a numeric caller gets `len=undefined` rendered in the input. The promised acceptance of number is not implemented by the body; this is an exported/public carrier, so the mismatch is a present defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Field input no longer contains caller's value, only a len= label
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior rendered the passed value into the uncontrolled input (defaultValue={value}). The new body replaces it with `len=${value.length}`, so the input now holds, e.g., `len=abc` for `value="abc"` — the actual data is dropped from the rendered element. Any consumer reading input.value (uncontrolled form submission, onChange of the host form, serialization) receives the derived label instead of the user's data, corrupting whatever is later submitted or persisted. The prop is still named `value` and the component is exported, so the value-passing contract is silently changed under an unchanged signature.

findings.title: value widened to number but value.length is undefined for numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported FieldProps.value type was widened from string to string | number (line 2), publicly promising Field accepts numbers. The body reads value.length (line 6): number primitives have no .length property, so it evaluates to undefined and the template literal renders `len=undefined` as the input's default value. Every caller that follows the new type and passes a number gets a broken field; only the string branch works. The promise ('number accepted') is not implemented by the body — a contract drift in a public, exported signature. (Under a strict tsconfig TypeScript would flag Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number', but the repo has no tsconfig and runtime behavior is wrong regardless.)

findings.title: Remove debug step that echoes deploy token into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` writes the full secrets.TOKEN value into the persisted Actions run log, visible to everyone with read access to the repo. GitHub's log masking is a best-effort backstop, not a control (it can fail on truncated/mangled values, is bypassable in exported/debug logs, and the docs explicitly instruct never to print secrets). The step is also functionally dead: the env:TOKEN block is scoped to the echo step only, so the token never reaches `make build` (line 13), and nothing in the workflow actually deploys — the step only exists to print the credential.

findings.title: Deployment secret is echoed into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step binds TOKEN to ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the raw secret value into the GitHub Actions log stream. Logs are retained and downloadable by anyone with repo access (public repos: anyone), and GitHub's automatic *** masking is best-effort — it is documented to fail for values containing newlines, non-UTF-8 bytes, or when output is transformed, so the deploy credential can land in persistent, shared artifacts. The step performs no deployment and the token is consumed nowhere else: `env:` is scoped to this single step, so the following `make build` step does not receive TOKEN, and rg confirms no other reference to TOKEN or secrets.TOKEN anywhere in the repo. The only effect of this PR is dumping the credential into logs; the step should be removed (if the token is genuinely needed, pass it via env only into the step that actually uses it, never into a run string).

findings.title: Secret TOKEN echoed into persistent CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step binds the deployment secret to the env and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, which writes the token value into the workflow log. GitHub's automatic log redaction of secrets is explicitly best-effort: values containing newlines or certain special characters are only partially masked or not masked, so the deploy credential can end up in retained logs readable by anyone with read access to the repo (and fully public if the repo is public). Additionally, `env` at step level is scoped to this step only, so `make build` on line 13 receives no TOKEN — the only consumer of the secret in this diff is the echo itself, meaning the change's sole effect is exposing the token rather than making it available to the deployment.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: >1MB git output now ENOBUFS-fails
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024 (1MB); the old code set 64MB. git() is the sole producer of the PR patch via `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) plus diff --name-only (line 57) and merge-base calls. On any output >1MB, spawnSync returns status=null with res.error=ENOBUFS and empty stderr (verified empirically: 1.1MB stdout -> status=null, error=ENOBUFS, stderrLen=0). Line 38's `res.status !== 0` then throws `git diff ... failed:` with a blank reason, runGithub's catch posts a failing check run ('Review errored and did NOT pass this PR') and exits 1. Real repos routinely produce >1MB diffs (lockfile bumps, generated/vendored files, large refactors), so a PR that previously reviewed fine now hard-fails — while gh() and ghText() still keep the 64MB buffer, making this look like an accidental deletion rather than a policy change.

findings.title: Restore 64MB maxBuffer: >1MiB diffs now abort the review run
findings.whyItBreaks: The removal of `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` re-imposes Node's default 1,048,576-byte cap on stdout+stderr for every `git()` capture. The one call that can realistically exceed it is `patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` at line 140 (also `diff --name-only` at line 57 for huge trees). Verified empirically on Node 24: a >1MiB output makes spawnSync kill the child with `status: null` and `error.code: ENOBUFS`. At line 38 `null !== 0` is true, so git() throws `git diff ... failed`; the catch in runGithub (~line 176) then posts a failing check-run 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR' and exits 1. Net effect: any PR whose patch exceeds ~1MiB (large refactors, lockfile/vendor/generated files — easily reached) gets no review at all, where the base commit handled up to 64MiB. The gh() and ghText() helpers (lines 19, 29) still carry 64MiB, confirming the removal is not a deliberate global policy change. Also, the failure is only discoverable at runtime on such PRs; nothing validates diff size.

findings.title: Bundle baseSha no longer matches the patch's actual diff base
findings.whyItBreaks: `patch` (line 140) and `changedFiles` (line 141) are computed against `mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` (line 139), and the previous code set `bundle.baseSha = mergeBase`, so the bundle was self-consistent: the reported base was exactly the commit the diff was computed against. The head now sets `bundle.baseSha = baseSha`, which is `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA` when set (line 138) — i.e. the base-branch tip, not the merge-base. Whenever the base branch has advanced past the fork point (the exact case merge-base exists for), `bundle.baseSha` is a commit that is NOT the base of the bundle's own patch: `patch = diff(mergeBase, headSha) != diff(baseSha, headSha)`. Every consumer of the Bundle that treats baseSha as the diff base (reporting the compared range, recomputing/verifying the diff, resolving base versions of changed files, or keying work on base..head) receives a base that contradicts the patch and changedFiles it is paired with, attributing base-margin commits to the PR. (In the fallback path — PR_BASE_SHA unset — the two are provably identical since merge-base is idempotent, so the regression is confined to the env-var path, which is the production Actions path.)

findings.title: Restore 64MB git maxBuffer; 1MiB default breaks large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now uses spawnSync's default maxBuffer of 1024*1024 bytes. All git output funnels through this helper, including `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140), which is the PR's full patch — routinely >1MiB for PRs touching lockfiles, vendored/generated files, or snapshots. When output exceeds maxBuffer, spawnSync returns status=null with error ENOBUFS (verified: status null, error.code ENOBUFS, stdout truncated), and `res.status !== 0` (line 38) then throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty/partial stderr. runGithub's catch block (lines 182-194) posts a failed check run and NO review — the PR is not reviewed at all. The base commit deliberately configured 64MB for this exact helper, and gh()/ghText() (lines 19, 29) still keep 64MB, so the removal is an inconsistent, likely accidental revert of a real safeguard.

findings.title: Restore -s read-only: sandbox now widens to workspace-write
findings.whyItBreaks: Before: `-s read-only` forced the sandbox regardless of environment. After: the flag is omitted, and codex 0.151 resolves the effective mode itself — verified chain: exec's CLI arg becomes `ConfigOverrides.sandbox_mode = None` (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:296-300, no config override or `--ignore-user-config` is passed by runCodex, so `~/.codex/config.toml` loads) → `derive_permission_profile` does `sandbox_mode_override.or(self.sandbox_mode)` and, if the directory has a codex trust record (`trust_level` Trusted or Untrusted — the normal state after a dev has run codex in the repo), defaults to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` on macOS/Linux (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs:749-767); only absent config/trust does `unwrap_or_default()` yield ReadOnly. Compounding this, headless `codex exec` hard-codes `approval_policy = AskForApproval::Never` (exec/src/lib.rs:411-413), so there is no prompt. Net effect: model-generated shell commands gain workspace-write access to `opts.repoPath` with no user interaction, where the previous code unconditionally denied writes. In a review harness this means the sub-agent can edit the repository it is reviewing; the wrapper's behavior also becomes non-deterministic across machines (same code, different sandbox depending on trust state/config), which is a regression on its own. Any write-access intent should be explicit (e.g. opt-in flag passing `-s workspace-write`), never implicit.

findings.title: Removing -s read-only lets codex write into the reviewed repo
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath and pipes the review prompt on stdin. The base pinned the model's sandbox to `read-only` with `-s read-only`; this change deletes that pin. Codex's own default derivation is not read-only: in codex (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs `derive_permission_profile`, ~L749-767, and codex-rs/core/src/config/permissions.rs `default_builtin_permission_profile_name`, ~L48-59), when no `-s/--sandbox` and no `sandbox_mode` config is set, any directory with a recorded trust decision (project is trusted OR untrusted in the `[projects]` table of `~/.codex/config.toml`, looked up by cwd or git repo root) resolves to `WorkspaceWrite`. So on any machine where codex has previously been run/trusted in the target repo — the common developer-machine case, and the docs call workspace-write 'the default low-friction mode for local work' — the agent invoked by this review helper gains write access to the repository under review and can modify source files, the reviewed diff, or run mutating commands without approval. The previous code made read-only an unconditional guarantee; the new code makes it depend on per-machine trust state. This cannot be a deliberate fix for `--output-last-message`: that file is written by codex's CLI event processor (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs `EventProcessorWithJsonOutput::new(last_message_file)`, ~L682), not by the sandboxed model commands, so read-only mode never blocked it.

findings.title: Dropped read-only sandbox pin from codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `-s read-only` from the args array, which was the only thing forcing codex into a read-only sandbox regardless of the host environment. In codex-cli 0.151.0 (the version in this environment), `--sandbox/-s` takes `read-only | workspace-write | danger-full-access` with no CLI default shown in `codex exec --help`, meaning the value is loaded from `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` key `sandbox_mode` (config.toml is applied whenever the flag is absent; the binary exposes `sandbox_mode` as a ConfigToml field and treats `read-only` as the fallback). So on any host whose `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"` — a very common setup for coding agents — the model-generated shell commands spawned by runCodex now execute with write/full-access permissions where they were previously hard-pinned read-only. runCodex is an exported public API that feeds its `prompt` (repo content/diffs of the PR under review — untrusted input) to an agent that runs arbitrary shell commands in non-interactive exec mode (no approval prompts), so prompt-injection in a reviewed diff can now modify the repository being reviewed or the host filesystem. The prior explicit flag existed precisely to make the sandbox independent of ambient config; this change removes both the guarantee and the determinism.

findings.title: Diff no longer merge-base normalized; PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA overrides feed wrong patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code computed mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha; the new code diffs baseSha..HEAD with no normalization. Two concrete failure modes, both previously guarded by the removed lines: (1) If the harness sets PR_BASE_SHA from github.event.pull_request.base.sha (the base branch TIP, which is the natural value for that env var) and main advanced after the PR forked, baseSha is NOT an ancestor of HEAD: `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes base-only commits as inverted changes, so patch and changedFiles list files the PR never touched. That pollutes surface classification and findings; inline comments on such files get rejected by the API and the catch fallback silently drops ALL inline comments. (2) headSha is still read (line 137) and used as commit_id for postReview/postCheck (lines 178-185) but is no longer the diff endpoint: if the checkout is not the PR head (e.g. pull_request_target-style checkout of the base branch), the analyzed patch is of the wrong tree — and if HEAD equals the base tip, `git diff baseSha HEAD` is empty, so the run reviews an empty diff and posts a check attributed to a commit it never reviewed. In the no-env-var path behavior is unchanged; the regression only fires when the override values the code explicitly accepts don't coincide with the local defaults, which is precisely why merge-base(baseSha, headSha) existed.

findings.title: Drop of merge-base + HEAD swap mis-scopes review diff for stale PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: Old: mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha); patch = diff(mergeBase, headSha); changedFiles = changedFileSet(cwd, mergeBase). New: patch = diff(baseSha, "HEAD"); changedFiles = changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) (helper at line 56 also diffs against literal HEAD). Substitution: the whole point of the removed merge-base call was that PR_BASE_SHA (GitHub base.sha semantics = base branch tip) is generally NOT an ancestor of the PR head once main has advanced past the fork point — the normal state of a live PR. In that state, diff(base tip, HEAD) contains the reverse of every base-only commit as spurious deletions, and changedFileSet returns the union of base-only and PR files. Consequences on a live path: (1) the review engine analyzes a patch that includes changes the PR never made and misses attribution; (2) changedPaths (line 141) now includes base-only files, so inlineComments (lines 61-70) can attempt comments on lines outside the PR's actual diff, which the GitHub API rejects with 422; postReview's catch (lines 92-96) only re-encodes the same POST, so the error propagates to runGithub's catch (lines 181-190) and the PR gets a "review failed" check instead of a review. Separately, headSha (PR_HEAD_SHA) is still used as commit_id/head_sha (lines 178-179, 184) but no longer feeds the patch/changedFiles computation: whenever PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout HEAD (e.g., checkout at refs/pull/N/merge with PR_HEAD_SHA = head.sha), the analyzed diff is not the diff of the commit the review is attached to. Default path (no env: baseSha = merge-base(origin/main, HEAD), headSha = HEAD) is provably unchanged, so the regression is confined to the env-var override path — but that is the path this adapter exists for (the default fallback requires origin/main and fails in a PR-only checkout).

findings.title: Removed merge-base makes patch include non-PR base-branch hunks
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code computed mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha; new code diffs baseSha..HEAD (two-dot) directly, assuming PR_BASE_SHA is already the fork point. PR_BASE_SHA (line 138) is the GitHub PR base ref tip, and after the base branch advances the tip is NOT an ancestor of the PR head — reproduced in a scratch repo: base tip B, head P forked from A, merge-base(B,P)=A; `git diff B P` emits mainfile.txt (touched only by base after the fork) as a DELETION plus the real PR change, while `git diff A P` shows only the PR change; `git diff --name-only B P` also lists mainfile.txt. Concretely: the patch handed to review() and the changedFiles/classifyFiles set (line 140) then contain hunks the PR never made, so the agent can flag the PR for 'reverting' base-branch commits and produce a wrong changes_requested verdict; inline comments can target lines on files not in the PR's real diff (the existing catch in postReview then silently drops all comments). A secondary drift: the patch is now computed against HEAD while postReview/postCheck still anchor on headSha (lines 137, 176, 196), so if the checkout is not exactly PR_HEAD_SHA the reviewed patch and the reported commit_id diverge. Note the default no-env path (baseSha = merge-base(origin/main, HEAD)) is unchanged and equivalent — but the env-var path this code explicitly supports is now wrong whenever the base has moved past the fork point (the common unrebased PR).

findings.title: String replacement now interprets $ patterns, corrupting model prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: All three substitutions were changed from a function replacer (verbatim insertion) to a plain-string replacement, so ECMAScript GetSubstitution now interprets $ patterns inside the inserted content. Any bundle containing '$$', '$&', "$'", or '$` (highly plausible: bundle.patch is raw diff text of arbitrary repo code — bash PID `echo $$`, bash ANSI-C `$'...'`, sed/awk `$&`, shell backticks; candidate JSON is LLM output that can quote such code) is silently rewritten: '$$' -> '$' (char dropped), '$&' -> the '{{BUNDLE}}'/'{{PATCH}}' placeholder text injected into the data, "$'" -> the portion of the template AFTER the match spliced into the middle of the data, '$` -> the portion BEFORE the match spliced in. Verified by direct execution: payload 'echo $$ / sed s/x/$&/ / grep -q "$'x" f' becomes 'echo $ / sed s/x/===(BUNDLE)===/ / grep -q "x" f' with the string form, and is unchanged with the function form. The corrupted prompt is the sole input to runCodex at line 28/34, so the reviewer model reviews altered code and findings — silent wrong verdicts, a regression from the previously-correct function form (base SHA 0d683f5).

findings.title: String replacer mangles $ sequences in bundle/patch content
findings.whyItBreaks:
String.prototype.replace interprets $ patterns in a string replacement but inserts a function replacement literally. The diff (base 6fa4000 -> head bb6a617) replaces the arrow-function replacers with plain strings at lines 23-26, 32, and 33. Consequently, any $ sequence inside JSON.stringify(bundle,...), JSON.stringify(candidate,...), or bundle.patch (the PR diff, whose content the author does not control) is rewritten at substitution time: $& becomes the matched marker ({{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}}), $' becomes the entire prompt text AFTER the marker — injected raw (unescaped newlines/quotes) into the middle of the JSON, producing invalid JSON — and $$ collapses to a single $. Verified with node: content {"a":"x$&y$'z $$w"} substituted into "header
{{B}}:
tail" yields {"a":"x{{B}}y:
tailz $w"}: the marker is spliced in, the prompt tail is embedded inside the JSON string, and $$ lost a character. The substituted text is then handed to runCodex, so the model sees corrupted data; when the JSON breaks, extractJson cannot parse it, and even when it survives the verdict can be wrong. The base code used ()=>JSON.stringify(...) precisely to avoid this, so this PR is a regression, and it hitches a route with the most uncontrolled input (bundle.patch) plus two JSON blobs.

findings.title: String replace() form corrupts prompt on $-sequences in patch/bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR converts `repl` from a function (used verbatim) to a plain string. With a string replacement, `String.prototype.replace` interprets the replacement's special `$` patterns against the matched `{{...}}` placeholder: `$$` collapses to `$`, `$&` becomes the placeholder text itself (e.g. `{{PATCH}}`), `$'` splices in the entire template tail that follows the placeholder, and `` $` `` splices in everything before it. JSON.stringify does not escape `$`, so any `$` sequence in bundle.patch (raw diff text — Makefile `$$`, bash `$'...'` ANSI-C quotes, sed `$&`), in bundle fields, or in the LLM-generated candidate findings JSON (which quotes reviewed code) is silently rewritten before the prompt reaches runCodex. Verified in Node: `t.replace("{{PATCH}}", "echo $$ > /tmp/x")` yields `echo $ > /tmp/x` on the new form but keeps `$$` on the old function form; `$'`/`$&` splice placeholder/tail text into the payload. Effects are silent — no error is raised, the model just reviews a corrupted patch (wrong verdicts, failed JSON extraction), on the core review path. The old `() => ...` form blocked all `$` interpretation and was correct.

findings.title: Restore validation: malformed findings now silently become fabricated defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw descriptive errors for non-object input, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite or <=0 lineStart/lineEnd (base lines 96-128). The rewrite (head 95-111) discards every one of those checks and substitutes placeholders: invalid/missing severity -> "P1" (head:98), missing title -> "Untitled finding" (head:99), invalid category -> "bug" (head:102), missing file -> "" (head:103), missing lineStart/lineEnd -> 0 (head:104-105) — and Number("abc") makes lineStart/lineEnd NaN with no Number.isFinite check. Concretely, model output {severity:"CRITICAL", category:"typo", file:"", lineStart:"abc"} now yields Finding{severity:"P1", category:"bug", file:"", lineStart:NaN} instead of raising 'invalid severity'/'missing file'/'invalid lineStart': a garbage severity is silently escalated to P1, a wrong category is silently reclassified, and a finding with no file/line is emitted as a valid finding. Nothing logs these substitutions, so any consumer of this exported API cannot distinguish malformed output from a genuine finding and will persist/report/verdict on the placeholder as if real (e.g. a fabricated P1 flipping a pass into changes_requested, or an empty-file finding breaking consumers that resolve paths). The same swallow applies to normalizeReview at head:131: old strict mode threw on malformed findings and old strict=false dropped them; now they are always fabricated (and a null element now throws a bare TypeError at head:96 instead of the descriptive error).

findings.title: Restore finite/positive guard for lineStart/lineEnd; NaN passes through
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code rejected non-finite or non-positive line numbers (Number.isFinite(lineStart) && lineStart > 0, base lines ~117-124). The new code does `Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0)` with no guard at all. Substituting: normalizeFinding({lineStart: "abc"}) returns lineStart: NaN (Number('abc') is NaN, and nothing sanitizes it); normalizeFinding({}) returns lineStart: 0, lineEnd: 0; normalizeFinding({lineStart: NaN}) also yields lineEnd: NaN via `raw.lineEnd ?? raw.lineStart ?? 0`. Finding is an exported public type whose lineStart/lineEnd anchor comments to source lines: any consumer doing 0-based conversion (lineStart - 1), an API line>=1 validation, range rendering, or sorting silently gets NaN (all NaN comparisons are false) or an invalid 0 anchor. Deterministic corrupt value from missing validation that the old code explicitly guarded.

findings.title: Malformed findings now masquerade as real P1 findings (error signal defaulted)
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeFinding previously propagated malformation as an error (base lines 95-134: throw on invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, bad lineStart/lineEnd), and normalizeReview had two modes: strict threw, non-strict dropped the malformed finding. Now every failure is mapped to a plausible default: invalid severity -> 'P1' (a blocking severity, worse: any typo like 'P4'/'PO' becomes a merge-blocking P1), missing title -> 'Untitled finding', missing file -> '', lineStart -> 0, whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> ''. A downstream consumer of normalizeReview can no longer distinguish an LLM-garbage finding from a genuine one, and acting on the fallback is unsafe: the fabricated P1 with file='' and lineStart=0 posts as a real high-severity review comment/gates the verdict, whereas before it either aborted or was dropped. Additionally, the removed `!raw || typeof raw !== 'object'` guard means a null entry in findings now dies with an opaque TypeError ('Cannot read properties of null') instead of the old clean error/drop, and the substitution happens silently with no warning signal for callers.

findings.title: Malformed findings silently become fabricated P1 entries instead of erroring or being dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: The change deletes every validation throw in the exported normalizeFinding and replaces them with defaults: invalid/missing severity -> "P1" (line 98), invalid category -> "bug", missing title -> "Untitled finding", missing file -> "" (line 103), lineStart/lineEnd -> 0 (lines 104-105). Previously (base lines 95-122) a malformed finding threw 'malformed finding: ...'; normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) defaulted to that throw (caller rejects/retries the model output), and the lenient path (base lines 157-165) dropped invalid entries entirely. Both paths are now gone (base line 137 'strict' param removed; head line 131 maps everything). Substituting real inputs: {severity:"HIGH", file:"a.ts", lineStart:1} previously threw; now returns {severity:"P1", file:"a.ts", ...} — a blocking-grade finding the model never emitted. {severity:"P2", title:"x", file:"a.ts"} previously threw (strict) or was dropped (lenient); now returns a finding with lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, whyItBreaks:"", suggestedFix:"" that is indistinguishable from a real finding. Additionally lineStart/lineEnd no longer get the isFinite/positive checks (base lines 115-121): Number("abc") -> NaN, which JSON.stringify emits as null, and negative values pass through. The exported contract (the only module in this repo, imported by the review harness) now forces every caller to conflate malformed model output with a real finding and to report/persist fabricated P1 findings; the distinguishing error signal was removed, not downgraded in a declared way.

findings.title: gh pr view without -R breaks manual workflow_dispatch trigger
findings.whyItBreaks: The REPO env var and -R "$REPO" were removed from `gh pr view`, leaving gh with no way to determine the target repo: GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not honored by gh (verified with gh 2.97.0: still fails), GH_REPO is not set, and no checkout exists yet (actions/checkout runs later at line 42). In a non-git directory, `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` exits non-zero with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository' (verified). The else branch (lines 37-40) is reached ONLY by workflow_dispatch — pull_request events always set EVENT_HEAD (line 34) — so the manual trigger is exactly the path broken. Because the failing substitution sits inside `echo "head=$(gh ...)"`, bash -e does NOT abort the step (verified: `bash -e -c 'echo "x=$(false)" >> /dev/null; echo alive'` prints 'alive', exit 0); it writes `head=`/`base=` (empty) to GITHUB_OUTPUT and the job continues. Downstream: actions/checkout receives ref:'' (line 45) and falls back to the event ref (default branch, not the PR head), and the Needlefish review step receives empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 56-57). So on any runner whose workspace is not a git repo at job start (always on hosted runners; any clean/first-run self-hosted runner), the manual review feature the workflow explicitly declares (on.workflow_dispatch with required pr_number) reviews the wrong ref with empty SHAs, and the gh failure signal is silently degraded to an empty value.

findings.title: gh pr view loses repo resolution: manual trigger emits empty SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The `else` branch is the ONLY path that runs `gh pr view` (EVENT_HEAD is set on pull_request events, so the changed lines execute exclusively on workflow_dispatch — the documented manual trigger, lines 10-14). This step runs before the "Checkout PR head" step (line 42), so the default working directory contains no .git and no git remote. With `-R "$REPO"` removed and no `GH_REPO` env var, gh has no way to determine the repository: it errors "failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository". gh does NOT fall back to GITHUB_REPOSITORY (verified locally: `GITHUB_REPOSITORY=foo/bar gh pr view 1` still fails with "not a git repository"; only `GH_REPO` resolves it). Because the failure happens inside `$(...)` with `echo "head=..."` succeeding, the step exits 0 and silently writes `head=` and `base=` empty. Downstream: `actions/checkout` (line 45) gets `ref: ${{ steps.refs.outputs.head }}` = empty and the review step (lines 50-51) gets empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, so the manual review does not run against the requested PR — and on a shared self-hosted runner the stale-workspace fallback could even resolve the wrong repo. Base commit had deterministic `-R "$REPO"` (with `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`), so this is a regression introduced by this PR.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for manual-dispatch gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch runs only on workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD is always set for pull_request events, and fork PRs are excluded by the job 'if' at line 24), and it executes BEFORE actions/checkout (line 42), so $GITHUB_WORKSPACE is whatever the self-hosted runner left behind — it is not guaranteed to contain a git repo, and on a fresh/cleaned runner it is empty. gh does not read the GITHUB_REPOSITORY env var (verified on gh 2.97.0: the binary contains zero 'GITHUB_REPOSITORY' strings; with only GITHUB_REPOSITORY set in a non-git dir, 'gh pr view' runs 'git remote -v', fails with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository' and never issues an API request — while GH_REPO is honored). Previously '-R "$REPO"' (REPO = github.repository) pinned the target unconditionally. Now: (a) empty workspace -> gh fails, and because 'echo "head=$(gh pr view ...)"' swallows the command-substitution failure under bash -e (verified: bash -e -o pipefail continues after 'echo "$(false)"'), the step silently writes empty head=/base= to GITHUB_OUTPUT, so checkout gets ref '' and the CLI gets empty PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA (lines 45, 56-57) — a silent broken review instead of a loud failure; (b) a stale checkout/remote pointing at a moved or renamed repo makes gh query the wrong repository, fetching the wrong PR's head/base SHAs and mis-routing the review. Restore the explicit repo via GH_REPO or -R.

findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops malformed findings, risking false pass
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `false` arg selects the lenient branch of normalizeReview (schema.ts:155-165): any finding that fails normalizeFinding (schema.ts:97-121 — bad severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, invalid lineStart/lineEnd) is caught and silently dropped (schema.ts:161-163), with no log and no count surfaced. The critic (prompts/critic.md) is prune-only ("Never add new findings"), so the dropped finding is gone for good; the only post-parse guard (review.ts:30) checks summary/checked, not findings. If the dropped finding was the sole blocker, the critic returns an empty findings list (critic.md explicitly welcomes it), deriveVerdict then returns "pass" (verdict.ts), and the GitHub adapter posts a SUCCESS check on the PR (github.ts:54-58, 184-186). In the base state the same malformed output threw, and the adapter posted a failure check with exit 1 (github.ts:188-196) — loud, no false pass. This diff is the exact inverse of upstream commit 49350eb ("fix: parse candidate strictly too; any malformed model output fails the review"), verified via git show: that commit removed precisely this `, false`. This is a silent error-signal loss on the review's core output path, not a style choice.

findings.title: Loose normalization silently drops candidate findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) at src/shared/schema.ts:137 (the base commit's module; review.ts matches upstream commit 094a271 except this one line) throws on any malformed finding (invalid severity/category, missing whyItBreaks, lineStart<=0, non-object). The default call in the base was strict, so a malformed candidate finding surfaced as a thrown 'malformed finding' error and review() aborted. Passing false selects the loose branch (schema.ts:156-165) which does try { normalizeFinding } catch { return null } and filters the nulls out with no signal whatsoever. The next stage makes this loss permanent: the critic prompt (prompts/critic.md) says its ONLY job is to PRUNE and to never add new findings, so a dropped finding is never recovered; the guard at review.ts:30-32 checks only summary and checked (not findings), so an output whose findings are all malformed passes straight through; and deriveVerdict over the pruned list can then return 'pass' (verdict.ts: deriveVerdict returns pass when no blocking finding remains). Net effect: when the model's candidate JSON has one malformed finding entry (realistic: category 'Bug'/'Security' casing, truncated whyItBreaks, lineStart 0), the review silently reports fewer or zero findings for a diff the model actually flagged — the caller receives a ReviewResult indistinguishable from a genuinely clean review, where the base behavior was a loud failure. The asymmetry with the critic call at line 38 (still strict, default true) shows this is not deliberate two-stage leniency.

findings.title: Candidate parse (strict=false) silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The imported normalizeReview(raw, strict=true)'s lenient branch maps every finding that fails normalizeFinding (non-object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, bad lineStart/lineEnd) to null and filters it out with no error and no log. Bug: a single missing required field kills the WHOLE finding. The usability gate at review.ts:30-32 only checks summary and checked, so an all-malformed findings list passes silently with findings:[]. The critic prompt (line 35) is built from JSON.stringify(candidate), so dropped findings never reach the critic; the final output's findings come from pruned.findings (line 48), and deriveVerdict returns 'pass' when no P0/P1/P2 finding and no blocking residual remains. Result: a PR carrying a real P1/P2 defect can be reviewed as a clean PASS. Before this change the default strict path threw on the same malformed finding, aborting loudly so the operator could retry; the change converts a visible failure into silent data loss. This is the same defect rejected in review on the real needlefish PR and later reverted by commit 49350eb ('fix: parse candidate strictly too; any malformed model output fails the review').

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output into blank review
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR deletes all five shape guards (non-object raw, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks) that threw 'malformed review output: ...' and replaces them with silent defaults (`?? []`, `?? ""`). Before: a caller (e.g. a harness parsing LLM output) could distinguish 'model returned garbage' via the caught exception and retry/fail loudly. After: `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview("text")`, or an object missing `summary` returns a structurally valid `RawReview` with `summary:""`, `findings:[]`, `checked:[]`, `residual_risks:[]` — indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review, so the caller will report/persist it as a real pass with no findings. Additionally, `String(raw?.summary ?? "")` coerces a non-string summary (e.g. an object → "[object Object]") instead of rejecting it, silently corrupting the review text. The function is exported, so the broken error contract ships even though nothing in this repo calls it yet. The repo contains only this file — there is no other validation point for review output, so removing these guards removes the only failure signal.

findings.title: Malformed review output silently normalized to empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Exportswed contract change: base threw Error("malformed review output: not an object") on null/non-object raw (base:115-117), on non-string summary (base:118-120), and on non-array findings/checked/residual_risks (base:121-131). Head deletes every guard: normalizeReview(null) now returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}, and {summary:42, findings:"x"} returns {summary:"42", findings:[], ...}. A review pipeline that feeds reviewer/LLM JSON through this (the module is the shared schema between reviewer and consumer) can no longer distinguish 'reviewer produced malformed output' from 'reviewer legitimately found nothing and passed' — the failure descends into an empty summary / zero-findings RawReview, which a consumer gating on findings.length or verdict would treat as a genuine pass. The defect ships in the exported contract now, independent of any in-repo caller; every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently accepts malformed output as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes all five malformed-output checks (base src/shared/schema.ts:115-131 threw 'malformed review output: ...' for non-object raw, non-string summary, and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks). Now any malformed input — null, prose string, JSON without the required keys — returns an apparently valid RawReview with summary:'', findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]. normalizeReview is exported and is the parsing entry for review output; the throw was the only signal a consumer had for 'the model produced garbage'. After this change, failure and a legitimate empty review are byte-identical: a caller that gates on findings/checked or renders/submits the review will silently act on failure-as-value (report a broken response as a clean pass, or persist a review that lost its checked evidence). For valid inputs the output is unchanged, but the error channel itself was removed from a public path.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path loses PR ref resolution; reviews wrong commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still declares workflow_dispatch with a required pr_number input (lines 10-14) whose stated purpose is to review a specific PR, but the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only code that resolved refs for that event. On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request.* is absent, so: (a) the Checkout step (line 29) evaluates github.event.pull_request.head.sha to '' and falls back to github.ref — the branch the workflow was dispatched from — instead of the target PR's head commit (old code: checkout used steps.refs.outputs.head resolved via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`); (b) PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) are empty strings, whereas the old code passed the gh-resolved headRefOid/baseRefOid; (c) BASE_REF falls back to 'main' (line 35), so the new 'Fetch base branch' step fetches refs/heads/main (wrong base, or a nonexistent ref in repos whose default branch isn't main, failing the job). Result: a manual dispatch review runs the CLI against the wrong working tree with empty base/head SHAs instead of the requested PR — exactly the case the old code's EVEN_HEAD-empty else-branch handled.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path broken: refs no longer resolved, empty SHAs passed to CLI
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step's else-branch used `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` precisely because on workflow_dispatch `github.event.pull_request` does not exist. The trigger and the required `pr_number` input (lines 11-16, unchanged) still advertise that manual path, but it is now fed three wrong values: (1) checkout uses `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` (line 29) — on dispatch head.sha is null, so the runner checks out `github.ref` (the branch/tag the dispatch was run against, e.g. main), NOT the PR head the user asked to review; (2) `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) resolve to empty strings, whereas the removed step passed the PR's actual base/head OIDs — the CLI at line 47 now runs `--github --pr N` with empty SHAs, so the requested PR is never diffed (it errors or diffs the wrong refs); (3) `BASE_REF` falls back to `'main'` (line 35) regardless of the PR's real base branch, so any PR targeting a non-main branch gets the wrong base fetched. Net effect: a manual dispatch no longer reviews the PR the operator specified — the workflow's documented manual trigger is a dead path.

findings.title: Restore PR head/base resolution for workflow_dispatch trigger
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still advertises workflow_dispatch support (if-condition line 24, pr_number input lines 10-14, CLI '--pr' fallback line 47), but the removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only code that handled it: when EVENT_HEAD was empty (dispatch), it resolved head/base/base_ref via 'gh pr view' (old lines 39-43). The replacement reads github.event.pull_request.* directly, which is EMPTY for workflow_dispatch events (the pull_request context is only populated for pull_request events). Consequences on manual dispatch: (1) line 29 checkout ref falls back to github.ref — the branch selected in the Run-workflow UI, not the PR head being reviewed; the PR's commits are never checked out; (2) line 35 BASE_REF falls back to 'main' regardless of the PR's actual base branch; (3) lines 45-46 pass empty-string PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to src/cli.ts, which the old workflow went out of its way to populate with real SHAs. The review either errors out (no base/head to diff) or silently reviews the dispatch branch instead of PR N — both are wrong behavior on a deliberately supported trigger.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: >1MiB PR diffs now abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper previously ran spawnSync with maxBuffer 64 MiB; the diff removes that option, so Node's default maxBuffer of 1024*1024 bytes (1 MiB) applies. The critical consumer is the live path at line 100: `patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` collects the entire PR diff. When git's stdout exceeds 1 MiB (common for lockfile updates, vendored/generated files, monorepo or asset-heavy diffs), Node's spawnSync does NOT throw — it returns `res.status === null` with `res.error = ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`. The guard at line 12 (`res.status !== 0`) treats null as failure and throws `git diff <sha> HEAD failed:` with an empty stderr, so runLocal aborts and no review is produced. The base commit supported diffs up to 64 MiB; this change removes that capability with no compensating size guard. The sibling gh() helper at line 36 still keeps 64 MiB, confirming the buffer was deliberate. Note that `git diff --name-only` (line 101) is also affected for repos with very large file counts, and `git config`/`merge-base` are fine. This is not a swallowed-error case (the failure still throws), but a plain capability regression on the tool's core path.

findings.title: Dropped maxBuffer caps git output at 1MB, breaking large-PR reviews

On any repo whose diff exceeds ~1MB (common: large lockfiles, vendored/generated files, big rewrites), spawnSync kills the child and returns status: null with error ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER; res.status !== 0 is then true, so the code throws 'git diff ... failed' (stderr likely truncated/empty, so the message misreports the cause). Line 100 is not inside any try/catch (unlike detectBase/repoSlug), so runLocal aborts and no review is produced — a hard regression from the base behavior where outputs up to 64MB succeeded. The sibling gh() helper at line 36 still keeps 64MB, showing the cap was deliberate for the same class of large output. Note the failure is not silent (it throws), but it converts a previously-supported input into a deterministic workflow failure with a misleading error.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large diffs fail with ENOBUFS

findings.title: Crash path posts check-run as neutral, losing failure signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block that reports a review crash posts a check-run named "Needlefish" with conclusion changed from "failure" to "neutral" (line 191). VERDICT_CONCLUSION already maps the legit needs_human verdict to "neutral" (line 53), so after this change a crashed review is indistinguishable, at the check conclusion level, from a review that ran successfully and asked for human attention: same check name, same conclusion, same grey/neutral status. The only remaining distinction is buried in the check title/summary. The summary text even says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", while the neutral conclusion does not convey failure to any automation reading the check (branch protection or status-based tooling that previously saw a hard red "failure"). The error signal that previously reached the PR is defaulted to the same value used for an in-band, non-error outcome, so a crash can silently look like "review ran, no blocker found, human needed" to anyone gating on the check conclusion. TRIGGER D derivations: swallow=github.ts:187-194 (conclusion field), signal=check-run failure conclusion, previously_reached=base file line ~186 ("failure"), now_receives="neutral", callers=[GitHub PR checks UI / branch-protection automation reading conclusion — distinguishable=no; same conclusion as needs_human outcome on line 53]. The job still exits 1, but the PR-facing signal is lost and the check's own summary contradicts its conclusion.

findings.title: Error path check-run conclusion downgraded failure→neutral, conflating crash with needs_human verdict

The summary text on the same check still claims "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", directly contradicting a neutral conclusion that means "neither passing nor failing". The stderr write and exitCode=1 remain, so the Actions job still fails, but the public check-run contract — the signal branch protection and automation actually consume — no longer reports the failure, and the machine-readable output.title ("Needlefish: review failed") is the only remaining distinguisher, which gate logic does not read.

findings.title: Keep review-error check conclusion at failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block now posts the 'Needlefish' check run with conclusion 'neutral' instead of 'failure'. GitHub's current docs (About protected branches) state: 'Required status checks must have a successful, skipped, or neutral status before collaborators can make changes to a protected branch.' So neutral SATISFIES a required check while failure does not: previously a review-infra error made the required 'Needlefish' check fail and blocked the merge, consistent with the summary text (line 193) 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR'; now the same error yields a passing conclusion and the PR can merge with NO review verdict at all. findings.title: Derive changed-file set from the same revision as the patch

Any mismatch between the two states (base advanced past the merge ref's base, push landed between workflow trigger and the gh call, or the checkout is not the merge ref / is the base ref) makes a file in the patch absent from changedPaths, so inlineComments' filter (line 63, changedPaths.has(f.file)) silently drops every comment for that file — no error, no fallback — while converse files show as changed with no hunks. findings.title: PR now controls its own review tool; restore pinned main checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow (da93ea4) checked the review tool out from frankekn/needlefish@main into needlefish/ (base lines 51-56), installed it there (base 58-61), and ran '$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/needlefish/node_modules/.bin/tsx' with cwd=target (base 64-72) — the PR head under review was only read, never executed, and its code could not alter the tool. The deleted comment stated this explicitly: 'This prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' The new workflow checks out the PR head (lines 43-47), runs 'pnpm install --frozen-lockfile' from the PR's package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml (line 51: PR-controlled preinstall/postinstall/prepare hooks and dependency build scripts execute on the runner), and runs the PR's own 'src/cli.ts' (line 59) with GH_TOKEN=${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} in env (line 56). Workflow permissions grant that token pull-requests: write and checks: write (lines 17-19), the job runs on 'runs-on: self-hosted' (line 23), the job 'if' permits any same-repo PR (head repo == this repo, line 24) to auto-trigger on opened/synchronize, and for pull_request events GitHub runs the workflow file from the PR head itself. Net effect: a malicious PR can (a) make the needlefish-review check report success unconditionally or emit a favorable review — bypassing the review gate this workflow exists to enforce; and (b) execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner with a write-capable GitHub token and the checkout's persisted credentials (actions/checkout default persist-credentials: true), e.g. exfiltrate the token or tamper with other PRs' reviews/check-runs. This is the identical attack the removed trusted-tool pattern was designed to prevent, and the comment claiming 'self-review mode' is required for this repo does not hold — the old pattern (tool pinned to main, PR as read-only target) works for this repo too; the PR's own tool changes only need to be exercised if the maintainer chooses to run them, e.g. via manually approved workflow_dispatch.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed: 'p1' silently downgraded to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code did String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES.includes check, so any case/whitespace variant of a legit severity ('p1', 'P1 ', 'P0\n') normalized to the true severity. New code tests the raw value with strict === against SEVERITIES, so those variants now fail the check and the branch silently emits 'P3' (lowest severity). normalizeFinding is an exported public path whose contract is to normalize possibly-malformed model output (the prior normalization code is the evidence of that contract); a caller-visible field (severity) now changes value for inputs that previously round-tripped correctly — a severity regression that can flip a critical finding to lowest-priority with no error, log, or warning. The simultaneously changed fallback P1→P3 is plausibly intentional, but the removal of trim/toUpperCase is collateral: it converts previously-valid inputs into fallback hits.

findings.title: Silent severity downgrade: non-exact values now map to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity) now compares raw values directly. Substituting the input class the old code explicitly supported: raw.severity = 'p2' → old path String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase() = 'P2' ∈ SEVERITIES → published as P2; new path includes('p2') = false → falls to the hard-coded 'P3'. Same for ' P1 ' (old P1 → new P3) and 'p0' (old P0 → new P3). Missing severity also flips from the old P1 default to P3. Every finding produced by the model passes through this slot via normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132), so a P1/P2 finding emitted with any casing or whitespace variance is silently published as P3 — no error, no warning — destroying the distinction between 'the model meant P3' and 'the model's value was malformed' and under-weighting real issues in the pipeline output. The removed trim/toUpperCase is direct in-repo evidence that non-exact casing was an expected input property.

findings.title: Severity normalization regression: 'p1' resolves to P3; fallback default flipped to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code stringified, trimmed and uppercased raw.severity before validating it, so 'p1', ' P0 ', or any casing/whitespace variation resolved to its canonical severity. The new code tests SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) on the raw value, so any non-canonical input (lowercase 'p0'/'p1'/'p2', trailing spaces — typical in LLM JSON output that normalizeReview parses as `any`) is rejected and lands in the fallback. Two compounding changes: (1) inputs that previously resolved to P0/P1/P2 are now downgraded to the fallback; (2) the fallback itself was changed from 'P1' to 'P3'. Substitution check: normalizeFinding({severity:'p1'}) -> String('p1').trim().toUpperCase()='P1' -> included -> 'P1' at base; head: SEVERITIES.includes('p1')=false -> 'P3'. A critical finding ('p0' lowercase) is silently reclassified as P3 at the shared schema boundary that every review path goes through (normalizeReview @ src/shared/schema.ts:132).

findings.title: Re-expose GitHub tokens to codex subprocess by dropping env scrub
findings.whyItBreaks: Base built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync (base lines 23-30). The diff deletes that block, and spawnSync without an `env` option defaults to process.env (Node docs: 'Default: process.env'), so the `codex exec` child now inherits all three GitHub credentials. The child is an LLM agent running with cwd=opts.repoPath (the repo under review) on a caller-supplied prompt; `-s read-only` only restricts writes — the agent can always read its own environment and can act on prompts injected via repository content. This was a deliberate credential-cleanup boundary and the PR removes it without replacement, turning any future exfiltration vector into full token exposure.

findings.title: Removed credential scrub leaks GitHub tokens to codex agent subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the env sanitization that deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN from the child environment. With `env` omitted, spawnSync inherits the complete parent process.env (Node documented default), so all three GitHub credentials now reach the `codex` subprocess. That subprocess is an LLM agent driven by an arbitrary prompt via stdin (`input: prompt`), built from the repo under review — i.e., untrusted third-party content. `-s read-only` only restricts filesystem writes; the process still has network access (required for the model API), so a prompt-injected repo can instruct the agent to read `$GITHUB_TOKEN` and exfiltrate it or use it for authenticated GitHub API calls (private data, gists, forks, Actions). The base commit deliberately scrubbed these exact three vars; this change silently reverses that existing security control with no replacement, scoping, or documented rationale.

findings.title: Removed env scrub leaks GitHub tokens into codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block deliberately built a sanitized env without GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The new code drops `env:` from spawnSync, so the child inherits process.env verbatim (spawnSync default). runCodex is an exported API that executes the codex LLM agent with a prompt derived from repository content — an untrusted input that can prompt-inject the agent. The codex subprocess and any tool/MCP server it invokes (and any CODEX_BIN override) can now read the caller's GitHub credentials from its environment and exfiltrate or abuse them (repo-scoped or user-scoped writes/reads); under CI this is the very token used to fetch the target repo. The removed lines were an explicit credential boundary, and this deletion removes it without a replacement, so the failure mode is a credential exposure regression, not an internal-only concern.

findings.title: Fork PRs now run untrusted code on the self-hosted runner (RCE)
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing preventing fork PRs from reaching this job. The workflow triggers on `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened), which fires for forks, `runs-on: self-hosted` (the maintainer's machine), checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (fork-owned, untrusted), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (arbitrary dependency install scripts from the fork's lockfile) and executes the fork's own source via `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr <n>`. Any fork PR now gets arbitrary code execution as the runner user on the self-hosted host (host credentials, ~/.ssh, runner registration creds, network) with no review gate. Because this is a `pull_request` event, the workflow definition used is from the PR's merge ref, so the fork can also rewrite this very workflow's steps. `permissions:` does not mitigate this: it limits the GITHUB_TOKEN, not host access; fork PRs get a read-only token anyway (making the CLI's check-run writes fail, but the host compromise is the actual exposure). This is the canonical GitHub-documented self-hosted-runner hazard: never run untrusted PR code on self-hosted runners.

findings.title: Fork PRs now execute untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` (base line 19) was the only control preventing fork-triggered runs. `pull_request` events DO fire for fork PRs, so any fork PR now runs this job on `runs-on: self-hosted`, which checks out the fork's head (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` @line 23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (executing the fork-controlled package.json lifecycle scripts @line 28), and directly executes the fork-controlled `src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN` set (@lines 30-34). A fork author can therefore run arbitrary code on the shared self-hosted runner (the classic pwn-request: RCE on trusted infra, access to filesystem/network/other credentials, and the repo GITHUB_TOKEN). The guard removal is exactly what GitHub docs warn against for self-hosted runners, and no src-side or second-workflow guard exists to compensate. Secondary effect: even on the intended path, fork triggers get the read-only fork GITHUB_TOKEN, so the `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` permissions are not honored and the review itself cannot be posted for fork PRs (403), while the job still executes and fails/clutters — but the runner compromise is the blocker.

findings.title: Removed fork guard allows untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only protection stopping PRs from forks. The workflow still triggers on `on: pull_request` (line 8), which fires for fork PRs, and `types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]` re-runs on every fork push. Without the guard, a fork PR now: (1) checks out the fork's own `head.sha` (line 23), (2) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) against fork-controlled package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml — frozen-lockfile only checks the two files agree with each other, so a fork simply modifies both to add a malicious dependency with lifecycle scripts — and (3) executes the fork's own `src/cli.ts` via `tsx` (line 34, the workflow comments confirm 'the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool'), all on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) with `GH_TOKEN` in the environment (line 33). This gives any fork author arbitrary code execution on the maintainer's self-hosted runner machine (internal network, runner-host credentials, cached state) — the classic pwn-request scenario. Even the repo-level 'require approval for first-time contributors' setting does not neutralize this: known/approved contributors re-run automatically, and approving means rubber-stamping code execution on your own infrastructure. If fork-PR review is the goal, the fork code must never be executed: review forks via `pull_request_target` with the tool checked out from a pinned base ref and the PR diff consumed only as data, on a GitHub-hosted (or isolated/throwaway) runner with no secrets — not the self-hosted machine.

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs rejects 0, silently overriding explicit env config
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard change from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` means `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` no longer yield 0ms — they now silently fall back to 5000ms and 2000ms. 0 was deliberately accepted before (negative values were already rejected, so 0 was the distinct 'no grace / give up immediately' setting). A user or CI configuration that already sets either variable to 0 to force immediate SIGKILL escalation (line 117-124: hardKillTimer after RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS, giveUpTimer after RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, both initialized from these constants at lines 3-10) silently changes behavior on upgrade: every hang now costs an extra ~5s (plus up to 2s) before the process is abandoned, with no warning. This is a silent config/behavior change on a user-facing env surface, not a bug fix — zero is a meaningful value for both timers.

findings.title: Rejecting "0" env value silently falls back to default delays
findings.whyItBreaks: The only inputs to readRunnerDurationMs are NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (fallback 5000, line 4-5) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (fallback 2000, line 8-9), used live in the timeout path at lines 123-124. Before this PR, Number("0") passed `parsed >= 0` and returned 0; now `parsed > 0` rejects 0 and silently substitutes 5000/2000. An operator who sets the env var to "0" (e.g. "no grace period, SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM" or "settle immediately after SIGKILL") gets a 5s/2s delay on every timeout instead of ~0ms, and 0ms is no longer expressible at all (any "0" yields the fallback, indistinguishable from an unset value). setTimeout(fn, 0) is valid, so no failure mode forced this tightening; it removes a legitimate configuration capability with no rationale, test, or doc change.

findings.title: Tail-coverage backstop removed: changed files can be silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted backstop (base lines 98-110) pushed any changed file not inside the selected hotspots into a 'tail-coverage' hotspot so it still got deep-reviewed, with the explicit guarantee 'never silently skip a changed file'. It is gone with no replacement. On the reviewLarge path (patch > 30000 chars or > 10 files), any changed file that the map pass did not assign to a surface, or that lives in a hotspot past the `slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` cut (mapper returns > 6 hotspots), now receives no deep review and no checked/residual note — the final review presents as complete while that file was never examined.

findings.title: Per-hotspot deep-pass failure now aborts entire large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch around each deep pass (base lines 122-132) was removed. Previously a throw from runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview for one hotspot was caught, recorded in `checked` plus a blocks:true residual naming the un-reviewed files, and the loop continued — the user still got the completed hotspots' findings and the critic pass. Now any single transient model failure in one of up to 6 sequential LLM calls propagates out of reviewLarge, discarding the map result, every already-completed hotspot review, and the critic pass: the review run produces no result at all instead of a partial review with an explicit blocking note.

A large-PR review whose deep passes flagged unresolved risk/coverage uncertainty now returns a clean verdict and empty risk list — the signal is replaced by a legitimate-looking empty value and is indistinguishable from 'deep passes found nothing to flag'.

findings.title: Removed tail-coverage backstop silently skips changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now takes only the top-6 risk-ranked hotspots and deep-reviews exactly those. The deleted block (base 2c8b01b:98-110) explicitly appended a 'tail-coverage' hotspot for any changed file not in a selected hotspot, with the comment 'never silently skip a changed file'. The map pass can leave files unmapped (the backstop's own why text says 'these changed files were not assigned to any surface'), and sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) drops files of any hotspot ranked below top-6. Both cases are now silently unreviewed: no hotspot entry, no unchecked entry, no residual risk, and the final review still returns a completed verdict — so a large PR can receive a review that claims completeness while entire changed files were never examined. Nothing in `checked` records the uncovered files either.

findings.title: One deep-pass failure now aborts whole large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch (base 2c8b01b:122-133) was removed. runCodex is an LLM call and its output passes through extractJson/normalizeReview, both of which throw on malformed output; the base code explicitly handled this by recording a blocks:true residual risk ('deep review of X failed; N file(s) not deep-reviewed') and continuing to the next hotspot. Now any single deep-pass failure (timeout, malformed JSON, empty summary) propagates uncaught out of reviewLarge — review() at line 138 has no catch — so the entire review of a large PR errors out with zero findings, even though earlier hotspots already produced validated findings that are lost, and the user gets no residual-risk note saying which files were not reviewed. Base behavior: review completes with partial findings plus a blocking residual risk. Head behavior: total failure on one flaky call.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop: changed files now silently skip deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: The coverage backstop (base lines 98-110) appended a 'tail-coverage' hotspot for every changed file not covered by the top-6 hotspots, with the explicit invariant 'never silently skip a changed file'. Head keeps `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93) and deletes the backstop with no replacement: any changed file that the map pass does not place in one of the 6 selected hotspots (files in the 7th+ hotspot, or files the surface mapper omitted) now gets zero deep review — no findings, no `checked` entry, no residual risk marking the gap. The PR can be returned as reviewed/PASS with whole changed files unexamined, and nothing signals the skip to the caller or user.

findings.title: One failing deep pass now aborts the entire large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch (base lines 122-131) isolated deep-pass failures: runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview throwing (or malformed LLM output, the same failure mode reviewSmall guards against at line 56-58) was recorded as a 'DEEP PASS FAILED' checked entry plus a blocks:true residual, and the remaining hotspots still produced findings. Head removes the catch, so any single failure in the up-to-6 hotspot loop propagates out of reviewLarge before the critic runs — the user gets no findings from the other hotspots, no 'which files were not reviewed' record, and no residual explaining the gap. findings.title: Large-PR path silently drops focus/deep options still honored by small path
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge (used when patch > 30000 chars or > 10 changed files, per isLarge at src/core/review.ts:73-75) no longer forwards bundle.focus/bundle.deep to the map pass (removed from mapBundle) and no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}} in the deep.md prompt (removed at src/core/review.ts:117-121). Meanwhile reviewSmall at src/core/review.ts:42-44 still serializes the entire bundle, including focus and deep, into the review prompt. Bundle.focus and Bundle.deep are live inputs of the same user-supplied bundle (same shape as the CLI context bundle), so the same options now have an effect on small PRs and none on large PRs: a --focus/--deep request is silently ignored exactly when the review is big enough to need steering, and the map pass can no longer bias hotspot selection or depth on the flag. The output quality/behavior for a large PR with focus set changes without any warning or error — a silent option regression. If the intent was to deprecate these options, they must be removed from reviewSmall and the Bundle contract too; leaving them honored on one path and dropped on the other is inconsistent.

findings.title: Large-PR path silently ignores focus/deep config
