findings.title: Large-PR review silently ignores --focus and leaves {{FOCUS}} in prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: The public --focus flag (src/cli/args.ts:57 'narrow the review lens') still populates Bundle.focus (schema.ts:59), but reviewLarge no longer forwards it. prompts/map.md:37 instructs the map pass to 'rank matching surfaces higher' when a focus field is set — the field is now absent from mapBundle, so focus surfaces are never prioritized (and with MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 slicing they may land in the low-priority tail). The deep pass lost its only focus instruction: the removed .replace('{{FOCUS}}', ...) was the sole consumer of deep.md:96 ('Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)'), so every deep prompt now contains a literal dangling '{{FOCUS}}' token and no focus guidance. reviewSmall never used focus (review.md has no FOCUS refs), so --focus is now a complete no-op across all paths. This is a silent contract violation: the CLI flag still advertises the behavior, nothing errors or logs, and the review completes unfocused.

findings.title: formatDuration emits "1m 60s" when seconds round to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes from the unrounded ms (Math.floor(ms/60000)) and then seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000), so the rounded seconds are never carried into minutes. For any duration in [n*60000+59500, (n+1)*60000) the output is "<n>m 60s": e.g. ms=119999 renders "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s", and ms=3599500 renders "59m 60s" instead of "60m 0s". This is fed into the rendered review report at both call sites (per-call stats line 75 and total duration line 80), so users of renderMarkdown see an invalid duration string. The previous implementation (round total seconds first, then decompose) was correct at these boundaries, so this PR is a regression, not a fix.

findings.title: formatDuration emits invalid "Xm 60s" when remainder rounds to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes = floor(ms/60000) and then rounds the remainder independently: seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000). When ms % 60000 is in [59500, 60000), seconds rounds to 60 but minutes is never carried. Concrete live outputs: ms=59500 -> "60s" (old: "1m 0s"); ms=119500 -> "1m 60s" (old: "2m 0s"); ms=3599500 -> "59m 60s" (old: "60m 0s"). The old implementation rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000)) and derived minutes/seconds from that, so seconds was always 0..59. The broken string appears in every rendered report: renderMarkdown line 75 formats each stat's durationMs and line 80 formats totalDurationMs, both fed by measured call durations which routinely land near minute boundaries. A user-visible "1m 60s" in the review report is a concrete wrong-output regression.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit '1m 60s' (seconds uncarried across minute rollover)
findings.whyItBreaks: New code computes minutes as floor(ms/60000) BEFORE rounding seconds, so when the sub-minute remainder rounds up to 60 the carry is lost: ms=59600 (59.6s) renders '60s' (old code: '1m 0s') and ms=119500 (1m 59.5s) renders '1m 60s' (old code: '2m 0s'). Every duration with remainder in [59.5s, 60s) of a minute renders with seconds=60 and an under-counted minute. This output is user-visible in the rendered PR review (renderMarkdown stats line, call sites at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80), so reviews can report e.g. '1m 60s · 2m 5s' with an impossible second value.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, contradicting its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so parsePositiveInteger("0", ...) now returns 0 instead of throwing. The unchanged carrier of this exported function still promises a positive integer: the identifier `parsePositiveInteger` and the error message "requires a positive integer" (line 33) both define positive as strictly > 0 (0 is non-negative, not positive). A caller that trusts the name to reject 0 (e.g. for retry counts, interval/delay values, or a worker pool size where 0 means 'run zero times' or disables a mechanism with no fallback) now receives 0 where the API explicitly advertises rejection. If allowing 0 was intended, the name and error message must change; if not, this is a silent validation regression — either way, the shipped contract no longer matches the implementation and the error message is now false for the newly-accepted value.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 (and blank input) despite 'positive' contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so the exported function parsePositiveInteger now returns 0 for "0" instead of throwing. Worse, Number("") and Number("   ") are both 0 (verified: empty: 0, spaces: 0), so blank/whitespace-only input — previously rejected with the error — now silently validates and returns 0. The function name and the error message at line 33 still promise 'a positive integer' (> 0), so callers receive a 0 count/manual value where the contract says a positive number is guaranteed; any caller that divides by it, sizes a loop, or treats 0 as a valid count gets a wrong result, and blank input is no longer distinguishable from an explicit 0. This is TRIGGER C: the public/exported carrier promises validation (positive, non-empty input) that the body no longer implements, and the promised behavior affects the result a caller receives.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, breaking its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `0` now passes an exported function named `parsePositiveInteger` whose own throw message still says 'requires a positive integer'. Worse, `Number('')`, `Number('  ')`, and `Number('-0')` all evaluate to 0 and are integer, so blank/whitespace input is now silently accepted and returned as 0 instead of rejected. No in-repo callers exist yet, but this is the module's public API (the repo's only source file), and every future caller parsing CLI/config values (e.g. timeoutMs, attempts) will receive 0 where the contract promised either a >=1 integer or an error — a value that most consumers interpret as 'no timeout'/'disabled', not as an error.
